children.title: Coordinate Charts
children.top_down_role: Local coordinate descriptions used to represent manifold neighborhoods.

knowledge_statements.title: Coordinate Charts
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional smooth-manifold chart with Euclidean coordinates.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(M\) be a topological manifold of dimension \(n\). A coordinate chart on \(M\) is a pair \((U,\varphi)\), where \(U\subseteq M\) is open and \(\varphi:U\to\varphi(U)\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) is a homeomorphism onto an open set. The components \(x^i=\pi_i\circ\varphi\) are the local coordinate functions, and each \(p\in U\) is represented by \(\varphi(p)=(x^1(p),\ldots,x^n(p))\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A coordinate chart identifies an open part of an n-dimensional manifold homeomorphically with an open subset of Euclidean space.
assumptions_latex: \(M\) is an \(n\)-dimensional topological manifold.
\(U\subseteq M\) and \(\varphi(U)\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) are open.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((U,\varphi)\) supplies local Euclidean coordinates on \(M\).

notation.meaning: coordinate chart with domain U and coordinate map phi

review_flags: auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition is mathematically standard, precise, and appropriate for the Coordinate Charts leaf, but no inspectable authoritative citation is supplied.

children.title: Compatible Atlases
children.top_down_role: Collections of compatible charts supporting global smooth structure.

knowledge_statements.title: Compatible Atlases
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Smooth compatibility and maximal atlases on finite-dimensional manifolds.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An atlas on an \(n\)-dimensional topological manifold \(M\) is a family \(\mathcal A=\{(U_\alpha,\varphi_\alpha)\}\) of charts satisfying \(M=\bigcup_\alpha U_\alpha\). It is smoothly compatible if, whenever \(U_\alpha\cap U_\beta\neq\varnothing\), the transition maps \(\varphi_\beta\circ\varphi_\alpha^{-1}\) and \(\varphi_\alpha\circ\varphi_\beta^{-1}\) are smooth on their open Euclidean domains. A smooth structure is a maximal smoothly compatible atlas.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A compatible atlas covers the manifold by charts whose overlap transformations are smooth; its maximal extension defines a smooth structure.
assumptions_latex: \(M\) is an \(n\)-dimensional topological manifold.
Each \((U_\alpha,\varphi_\alpha)\) is a coordinate chart on \(M\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathcal A\) determines a smooth structure precisely through smooth transition maps.
review_flags: auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The atlas and smooth-compatibility definition fits the leaf and is mathematically standard, but it has no authoritative source reference or specific locator.

children.title: Local Coordinate Calculus
children.top_down_role: Coordinate-level interfaces for local geometric calculations.

knowledge_statements.title: Local Coordinate Calculus
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Coordinate representation of differentials and tangent vectors.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F:M\to N\) be smooth, let \(p\in M\), and choose charts \((U,\varphi)\) at \(p\) and \((V,\psi)\) at \(F(p)\). The differential is represented in coordinates by \(D(\psi\circ F\circ\varphi^{-1})(\varphi(p))\). Thus a tangent vector with coordinate column \(v\) is mapped to the coordinate column \(D(\psi\circ F\circ\varphi^{-1})(\varphi(p))v\). Under chart changes, these columns transform by the corresponding transition-map Jacobians.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Local charts turn manifold differentials into ordinary Jacobian multiplication, with transition Jacobians governing changes of coordinates.
assumptions_latex: \(M\) and \(N\) are finite-dimensional smooth manifolds.
\(F:M\to N\) is smooth.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \([dF_p(v)]_\psi=D(\psi\circ F\circ\varphi^{-1})(\varphi(p))[v]_\varphi\).

notation.meaning: coordinate column of a tangent vector in chart phi

children.title: Tangent Bundle Structure
children.top_down_role: Organization of tangent spaces across the manifold.

knowledge_statements.title: Tangent Bundle Structure
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Smooth tangent bundle of a finite-dimensional manifold.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a smooth \(n\)-manifold \(M\), its tangent bundle is the disjoint union \(TM=\bigsqcup_{p\in M}T_pM\) with projection \(\pi:TM\to M\), \(\pi(v)=p\) for \(v\in T_pM\). For every chart \((U,\varphi)\), the map \(\Phi:\pi^{-1}(U)\to\varphi(U)\times\mathbb R^n\), \(\Phi(v)=(\varphi(p),d\varphi_p(v))\), is a bundle chart. These charts give \(TM\) a smooth \(2n\)-manifold structure and rank-\(n\) vector-bundle structure.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The tangent bundle collects all tangent spaces and is locally a product of a manifold chart with an n-dimensional vector space.
assumptions_latex: \(M\) is a smooth manifold of dimension \(n\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\pi:TM\to M\) is a smooth rank-\(n\) vector bundle and \(\dim(TM)=2n\).
review_flags: auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The tangent-bundle construction and bundle-chart description fit the leaf, but the smooth-manifold and vector-bundle assertions require an authoritative cited source with a specific locator.

children.title: Smooth Vector Fields
children.top_down_role: Smoothly varying tangent-vector assignments.

knowledge_statements.title: Smooth Vector Fields
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Smooth sections of the tangent bundle.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A vector field on a smooth manifold \(M\) is a section \(X:M\to TM\) of the tangent-bundle projection, so \(\pi\circ X=\operatorname{id}_M\) and \(X(p)\in T_pM\) for every \(p\in M\). It is smooth when \(X\) is smooth as a map into \(TM\). Equivalently, in every smooth chart with coordinates \((x^1,\ldots,x^n)\), there exist smooth functions \(X^i\) such that \(X=\sum_{i=1}^n X^i\,\partial/\partial x^i\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A smooth vector field assigns a tangent vector smoothly to every point, equivalently having smooth component functions in every chart.
assumptions_latex: \(M\) is a smooth \(n\)-manifold.
\(\pi:TM\to M\) is its tangent-bundle projection.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(X\) is smooth exactly when its coordinate components \(X^1,\ldots,X^n\) are smooth in every chart.
review_flags: auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition of a smooth vector field as a smooth section and its coordinate characterization are standard and suitable, but no inspectable source is cited.

children.title: Local Trivializations of Tangent Bundles
children.top_down_role: Local representations connecting bundle geometry with coordinates.

knowledge_statements.title: Local Trivializations of Tangent Bundles
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Chart-induced local product representation of the tangent bundle.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given a chart \((U,\varphi)\) on a smooth \(n\)-manifold \(M\), define \(\tau_U:\pi^{-1}(U)\to U\times\mathbb R^n\) by \(\tau_U(v)=(p,d\varphi_p(v))\) for \(v\in T_pM\). Then \(\tau_U\) is a diffeomorphism, is linear on every fiber, and satisfies \(\operatorname{pr}_1\circ\tau_U=\pi\). On an overlap, the fiber coordinate changes by \(w\mapsto D(\psi\circ\varphi^{-1})(\varphi(p))w\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A manifold chart identifies the tangent bundle locally with a product, and overlap maps act on tangent coordinates through transition Jacobians.
assumptions_latex: \(M\) is a smooth \(n\)-manifold.
\((U,\varphi)\) and \((V,\psi)\) are smooth charts.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(TM|_U\cong U\times\mathbb R^n\) as smooth vector bundles.

notation.meaning: restriction of the tangent bundle to U

children.title: Smooth Maps

knowledge_statements.title: Smooth Maps
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Coordinate definition of smoothness between manifolds.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(M\) and \(N\) be smooth manifolds. A map \(F:M\to N\) is smooth if, for every \(p\in M\), there are smooth charts \((U,\varphi)\) about \(p\) and \((V,\psi)\) about \(F(p)\), with \(F(U)\subseteq V\), such that \(\psi\circ F\circ\varphi^{-1}:\varphi(U)\to\psi(V)\) is smooth as a map between open subsets of Euclidean spaces. Compatibility of atlases makes this definition chart-independent.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A map between smooth manifolds is smooth when its expression in local coordinates is an ordinary smooth Euclidean map.
assumptions_latex: \(M\) and \(N\) carry smooth atlases.
\(F:M\to N\) is a map.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F\) is smooth exactly when its local coordinate representatives are smooth.

children.title: Immersion Geometry
children.top_down_role: Locally injective differential behavior relevant to represented submanifolds.

knowledge_statements.title: Immersion Geometry
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Immersions characterized by injective differentials.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(M^m\) and \(N^n\) be smooth manifolds with \(m\leq n\). A smooth map \(F:M\to N\) is an immersion at \(p\in M\) if its differential \(dF_p:T_pM\to T_{F(p)}N\) is injective, equivalently \(\operatorname{rank}(dF_p)=m\). It is an immersion if this holds at every point. Locally near each point, suitable coordinates put it in the form \((x^1,\ldots,x^m)\mapsto(x^1,\ldots,x^m,0,\ldots,0)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An immersion has injective differential everywhere and locally looks like the standard inclusion of a lower-dimensional Euclidean space.
assumptions_latex: \(M^m\) and \(N^n\) are smooth manifolds with \(m\leq n\).
\(F:M\to N\) is smooth.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F\) is an immersion if and only if \(\operatorname{rank}(dF_p)=m\) for every \(p\in M\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: immersion definition and constant-rank normal form
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

children.title: Submersion Geometry

knowledge_statements.title: Submersion Geometry
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Submersions characterized by surjective differentials.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(M^m\) and \(N^n\) be smooth manifolds with \(m\geq n\). A smooth map \(F:M\to N\) is a submersion at \(p\in M\) if \(dF_p:T_pM\to T_{F(p)}N\) is surjective, equivalently \(\operatorname{rank}(dF_p)=n\). It is a submersion if this holds everywhere. Locally near each point, suitable coordinates put it in the form \((x^1,\ldots,x^m)\mapsto(x^1,\ldots,x^n)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A submersion has surjective differential everywhere and locally looks like projection onto the first n coordinates.
assumptions_latex: \(M^m\) and \(N^n\) are smooth manifolds with \(m\geq n\).
\(F:M\to N\) is smooth.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F\) is a submersion if and only if \(\operatorname{rank}(dF_p)=n\) for every \(p\in M\).

knowledge_statements.title: Regular Level-Set Manifolds
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Regular-value theorem for Euclidean equality constraints.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^m\) be smooth, let \(c\in\mathbb R^m\), and suppose \(DF(x)\) has rank \(m\) for every \(x\in F^{-1}(c)\). Then \(M=F^{-1}(c)\) is either empty or an embedded smooth submanifold of \(\mathbb R^n\) of dimension \(n-m\). At every \(x\in M\), its tangent space is \(T_xM=\ker DF(x)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A level set with full-row-rank constraint Jacobian is an embedded manifold whose tangent space is the Jacobian kernel.
assumptions_latex: \(F:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^m\) is smooth.
\(c\in\mathbb R^m\) is a regular value of \(F\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(M=F^{-1}(c)\) is an embedded \((n-m)\)-manifold and \(T_xM=\ker DF(x)\) for every \(x\in M\).

knowledge_statements.title: Tangent–Normal Decompositions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Orthogonal splitting for embedded Riemannian submanifolds.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(M\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be an embedded smooth submanifold with the metric induced by the Euclidean inner product. For every \(x\in M\), define the normal space by \(N_xM=(T_xM)^\perp\). Then the ambient space has the orthogonal direct-sum decomposition \(\mathbb R^n=T_xM\oplus N_xM\). Consequently every \(z\in\mathbb R^n\) has unique components \(z_T\in T_xM\) and \(z_N\in N_xM\) satisfying \(z=z_T+z_N\) and \(\langle z_T,z_N\rangle=0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At each point of an embedded Euclidean manifold, every ambient vector splits uniquely into orthogonal tangent and normal components.
assumptions_latex: \(M\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) is an embedded smooth submanifold.
\(M\) has the metric induced by the Euclidean inner product.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathbb R^n=T_xM\oplus N_xM\) orthogonally for every \(x\in M\).

auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

knowledge_statements.title: Ambient Projection Representations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Orthogonal tangent and normal projectors for regular level sets.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(M=F^{-1}(c)\subseteq\mathbb R^n\), where \(F:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^m\) is smooth and \(J=DF(x)\) has full row rank at \(x\in M\). Since \(T_xM=\ker J\) and \(N_xM=\operatorname{range}(J^\top)\), the Euclidean orthogonal projectors are \[P_{N_xM}=J^\top(JJ^\top)^{-1}J,\qquad P_{T_xM}=I-J^\top(JJ^\top)^{-1}J.\] Thus any ambient vector \(z\) decomposes as \(z=P_{T_xM}z+P_{N_xM}z\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For full-rank equality constraints, tangent and normal projections are explicit matrix expressions involving the constraint Jacobian.
assumptions_latex: \(M=F^{-1}(c)\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) is a regular level-set manifold.
\(J=DF(x)\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\) has full row rank.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(P_{T_xM}=I-J^\top(JJ^\top)^{-1}J\) and \(P_{N_xM}=J^\top(JJ^\top)^{-1}J\).

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Euclidean equality constraints with full-row-rank Jacobian.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(\mathcal{M}=\{y\in U:c(y)=0\}\). The embedded constraint-qualification interface at \(x\in\mathcal{M}\) is the surjectivity condition \(Dc(x):\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^m\). Under this condition, \(\mathcal{M}\) is locally an embedded submanifold of dimension \(n-m\), and its first-order feasible and normal directions are
\[
T_x\mathcal{M}=\ker Dc(x),\qquad N_x\mathcal{M}=\operatorname{range} Dc(x)^{\mathsf T}.
\]
Thus ambient equality-constraint derivatives provide the tangent-normal interface used by manifold algorithms.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A full-row-rank constraint Jacobian makes the level set locally embedded; tangent directions lie in its kernel, while normal directions lie in its transpose range.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Smooth quotient theorem for free proper Lie-group actions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define \(x\sim y\) when \(y=g\cdot x\) for some \(g\in G\), and let \(M/G\) be the set of equivalence classes. If the smooth action of \(G\) on \(M\) is free and proper, then \(M/G\) admits a unique smooth-manifold structure such that the canonical map \(\pi(x)=[x]\) is a smooth surjective submersion. Each fiber satisfies \(\pi^{-1}([x])=G\cdot x\), and \(M\to M/G\) is a principal \(G\)-bundle.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A smooth, free, proper Lie-group action produces a smooth orbit manifold, with the orbit projection a surjective submersion and principal bundle.

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: vertical space is the tangent space to an orbit and kernel of the quotient differential
No relevant differential-geometry source locator was supplied; authoritative source required.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Vertical geometry of a regular group-action quotient.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(x\in M\), the vertical space is the tangent space to the fiber of the quotient projection:
\[
\mathcal{V}_x:=T_x\pi^{-1}([x])=T_x(G\cdot x)=\ker d\pi_x.
\]
Equivalently, if \(\mathfrak{g}\) is the Lie algebra of \(G\), then
\[
\mathcal{V}_x=\{\xi_M(x):\xi\in\mathfrak{g}\},
\]
where \(\xi_M(x)=\left.\frac{d}{dt}\right|_{t=0}\exp(t\xi)\cdot x\). Freeness makes the map \(\xi\mapsto\xi_M(x)\) injective.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The vertical space consists exactly of tangent directions along the group orbit, equivalently the kernel of the quotient projection differential.
knowledge_statements.title: Vertical Space Geometry

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The vertical-space definition and its equivalent orbit, kernel, and infinitesimal-action descriptions are appropriate, but no source locator is supplied.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Metric-orthogonal connection on a regular Riemannian quotient.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
At each \(x\in M\), define the horizontal space by
\[
\mathcal{H}_x:=\mathcal{V}_x^{\perp_g}=\{\eta\,\in T_xM:g_x(\eta,
u)=0\ \text{for every }\nu\in\mathcal{V}_x\}.
\]
Because \(d\pi_x\) is surjective with kernel \(\mathcal{V}_x\), its restriction \(d\pi_x|_{\mathcal{H}_x}\) is a linear isomorphism from \(\mathcal{H}_x\) onto \(T_{[x]}(M/G)\). Metric invariance makes the family \(x\mapsto\mathcal{H}_x\) equivariant along each orbit.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The horizontal space is the metric-orthogonal complement of the orbit directions and maps isomorphically onto the quotient tangent space.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Orthogonal splitting of total-space tangent vectors.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For every \(x\in M\), the vertical and horizontal spaces form the orthogonal direct sum
\[
T_xM=\mathcal{V}_x\oplus\mathcal{H}_x.

Consequently, each \(\eta\in T_xM\) has unique components \(\eta^{\mathcal V}\in\mathcal{V}_x\) and \(\eta^{\mathcal H}\in\mathcal{H}_x\) satisfying \(\eta=\eta^{\mathcal V}+\eta^{\mathcal H}\). knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every total-space tangent vector splits uniquely into orthogonal vertical and horizontal components, with complementary idempotent projections.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Quotient metric induced by an invariant total-space metric.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \([x]\in M/G\) and \(u,v\in T_{[x]}(M/G)\), let \(u_x^{\mathcal H},v_x^{\mathcal H}\in\mathcal{H}_x\) be their unique horizontal lifts. Define
\[
\bar g_{[x]}(u,v):=g_x(u_x^{\mathcal H},v_x^{\mathcal H}).
\]
Since the action is isometric, this value is independent of the representative \(x\) in its orbit. It therefore defines a Riemannian metric \(\bar g\) on \(M/G\), uniquely characterized by requiring \(d\pi_x|_{\mathcal H_x}\) to be an isometry for every \(x\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Measure quotient tangent vectors by their horizontal lifts. Isometric group action makes the resulting inner product independent of the chosen representative.
knowledge_statements.title: Quotient Metric Construction

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The horizontal-lift construction of the quotient metric is appropriate and mathematically standard, but representative independence and uniqueness require an inspectable source.

children.top_down_role: Objectives whose values respect representative equivalence.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Descent of differentiable objectives through a regular quotient.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The objective \(f\) is group invariant when \(f(g\cdot x)=f(x)\) for every \(g\in G\) and \(x\in M\). This holds exactly when there is a unique function \(\bar f:M/G\to\mathbb{R}\) satisfying \(f=\bar f\circ\pi\). If \(f\) is differentiable, invariance implies
\[
df_x(\nu)=0\qquad\text{for every }\nu\in\mathcal{V}_x.
\]
Hence, for any metric defining \(\mathcal{H}_x=\mathcal{V}_x^{\perp}\), the Riemannian gradient \(\operatorname{grad}f(x)\) is horizontal.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An objective descends to the quotient exactly when it is constant on every orbit; its derivative then vanishes in all vertical directions.
knowledge_statements.title: Invariant Objective Structure

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The invariant-objective characterization and vertical derivative consequence fit the container, but no source with a specific locator is supplied.

children.title: Metric–Invariance Compatibility
children.top_down_role: Structural compatibility between quotient metrics, symmetry, plus optimization objectives.

knowledge_statements.title: Metric–Invariance Compatibility
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Compatibility needed for representative-independent metric and gradient computations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Metric–invariance compatibility requires every action map \(\Phi_a(x)=a\cdot x\) to be an isometry and the objective to be orbit invariant:
\[
g_{a\cdot x}(d\Phi_a\eta,d\Phi_a\zeta)=g_x(\eta,\zeta),\qquad f(a\cdot x)=f(x).
\]
These identities must hold for all \(a\in G\), \(x\in M\), and \(\eta,\zeta\in T_xM\). They imply \(d\Phi_a(\mathcal{H}_x)=\mathcal{H}_{a\cdot x}\) and \(\operatorname{grad}f(a\cdot x)=d\Phi_a\operatorname{grad}f(x)\), so quotient metric and gradient computations do not depend on the representative.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An isometric group action and orbit-invariant objective make horizontal spaces and gradients transform equivariantly, ensuring representative-independent quotient computations.
assumptions_latex: \(G\) acts smoothly, freely, and properly on \(M\).
\(g_M\) is a Riemannian metric and \(f:M\to\mathbb{R}\) is differentiable.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(g_{a\cdot x}(d\Phi_a\eta,d\Phi_a\zeta)=g_x(\eta,\zeta)\) and \(f(a\cdot x)=f(x)\) ensure representative-independent quotient metric and gradient computations.

notation.meaning: Action diffeomorphism associated with a group element

children.title: Quotient Lifting Interfaces
children.top_down_role: Interfaces for representing quotient objects in a total space.

knowledge_statements.title: Quotient Lifting Interfaces
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Pointwise lifting of quotient tangent vectors to representatives.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(x\in M\), the restriction \(d\pi_x|_{\mathcal{H}_x}:\mathcal{H}_x\to T_{[x]}(M/G)\) is a linear isomorphism. The quotient lifting interface is therefore
\[
\operatorname{lift}_x:=\bigl(d\pi_x|_{\mathcal{H}_x}\bigr)^{-1}.
\]
For every \(u\in T_{[x]}(M/G)\), its lift \(u_x^{\mathcal H}=\operatorname{lift}_x(u)\) is uniquely characterized by \(u_x^{\mathcal H}\in\mathcal{H}_x\) and \(d\pi_x(u_x^{\mathcal H})=u\). Under an invariant connection, lifts at different representatives are related by the differential of the group action.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A quotient tangent vector has a unique horizontal lift at each representative, obtained by inverting the quotient differential restricted to the horizontal space.
assumptions_latex: \(\pi:M\to M/G\) is a regular quotient projection.
\(T_xM=\mathcal{V}_x\oplus\mathcal{H}_x\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{lift}_x=(d\pi_x|_{\mathcal{H}_x})^{-1}\) is the unique horizontal right inverse of \(d\pi_x\).

notation.meaning: Horizontal lifting map at a representative

No relevant manifold-optimization source locator was supplied; authoritative source required.

children.title: Horizontal Projection Interfaces
children.top_down_role: Interfaces for extracting horizontal components from representative-space data.

assumptions_latex: \(T_xM=\mathcal{V}_x\oplus\mathcal{H}_x\) is an orthogonal decomposition.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(P_x^{\mathcal H}\eta=\eta-P_x^{\mathcal V}\eta\) is the unique horizontal vector differing from \(\eta\) by a vertical vector.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: complementary orthogonal projections implement the horizontal representation interface
No relevant manifold-optimization source locator was supplied; authoritative source required.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Projection of total-space directions onto horizontal representatives.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For each \(\eta\in T_xM\), the horizontal projection is
\[
P_x^{\mathcal H}\eta:=\eta-P_x^{\mathcal V}\eta.
\]
Equivalently, \(P_x^{\mathcal H}\eta\) is the unique vector in \(\mathcal{H}_x\) such that \(\eta-P_x^{\mathcal H}\eta\in\mathcal{V}_x\). It satisfies \(d\pi_x(P_x^{\mathcal H}\eta)=d\pi_x(\eta)\), so removing a vertical component does not alter the represented quotient tangent vector. For an orthogonal splitting, \(P_x^{\mathcal H}\) is self-adjoint and idempotent with respect to the total-space metric.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Horizontal projection removes the vertical component of a tangent vector without changing the quotient tangent vector it represents.
knowledge_statements.title: Horizontal Projection Interfaces

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The horizontal projection representation is precise and fits the interface leaf, but it has no inspectable supporting citation.

children.title: Horizontal-Curve Representation
children.top_down_role: Curve representations that encode quotient motion through horizontal lifts.

knowledge_statements.title: Horizontal-Curve Representation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Unique maximal horizontal lifting of quotient curves.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A curve \(\gamma:J\to M\) horizontally represents \(\bar\gamma:I\to M/G\) when \(J\subseteq I\), \(\pi(\gamma(t))=\bar\gamma(t)\), and
\[
\dot\gamma(t)=\operatorname{lift}_{\gamma(t)}\bigl(\dot{\bar\gamma}(t)\bigr)\in\mathcal{H}_{\gamma(t)}.
\]
Given \(t_0\in I\) and \(x_0\in\pi^{-1}(\bar\gamma(t_0))\), the associated first-order lifting equation has a unique maximal solution with \(\gamma(t_0)=x_0\). Conversely, every horizontal curve projects to a quotient curve whose velocity is \(d\pi_{\gamma(t)}\dot\gamma(t)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A quotient curve is represented by the unique maximal lift through a chosen representative whose velocity remains horizontal and projects to the quotient velocity.
assumptions_latex: \(\pi:M\to M/G\) is a regular quotient equipped with a smooth horizontal distribution.
\(\bar\gamma:I\to M/G\) is continuously differentiable and \(x_0\in\pi^{-1}(\bar\gamma(t_0))\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: There is a unique maximal curve \(\gamma\) through \(x_0\) satisfying \(\pi\circ\gamma=\bar\gamma\) and \(\dot\gamma(t)\in\mathcal{H}_{\gamma(t)}\).

notation.meaning: Horizontal lift in the total space

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: horizontal lifting theorem for curves under an Ehresmann connection
Exact global existence hypotheses require an authoritative source; only the unique maximal-lift formulation is asserted.

children.title: Nonfree Group Actions
children.top_down_role: Orbit structures with nontrivial stabilizers.

knowledge_statements.title: Nonfree Group Actions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Concrete singular boundary caused by changing stabilizers and orbit dimensions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For the rotation action of \(G=SO(2)\) on \(M=\mathbb{R}^2\), the stabilizer is \(G_x=\{e\}\) when \(x\neq 0\), but \(G_0=SO(2)\). Thus the action is not free. Nonzero orbits are circles of dimension one, whereas the orbit of \(0\) has dimension zero. The orbit space is identified topologically with \([0,\infty)\) by \(q(x)=\lVert x\rVert\). The map \(q\) is smooth with rank one on \(\mathbb{R}^2\setminus\{0\}\) but is not differentiable at \(0\). Consequently, the free-action quotient theorem and regular principal-bundle representation do not extend across the exceptional orbit.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Planar rotations are free away from the origin but fix the origin. Orbit dimension changes there, and the radius quotient map ceases to be differentiable, so the regular principal-bundle quotient model fails across that orbit.
assumptions_latex: \(SO(2)\) acts on \(\mathbb{R}^2\) by planar rotations.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The orbit space is identified with \([0,\infty)\) by \(q(x)=\lVert x\rVert\); \(q\) has rank one away from \(0\) and is not differentiable at \(0\), exposing singular behavior at the exceptional orbit.

notation.meaning: Special orthogonal group in two dimensions

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: planar rotation action is the canonical nonfree-action singularity example
No relevant transformation-group source locator was supplied; authoritative source required.

children.title: Singular Quotient Strata
children.top_down_role: Nonsmooth or stratified regions arising in quotient spaces.

knowledge_statements.title: Singular Quotient Strata
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Orbit-type stratification of a proper, nonfree Lie-group quotient.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let a Lie group \(G\) act smoothly and properly on a manifold \(M\). For a closed subgroup \(H\leq G\), define the orbit-type subset \(M_{(H)}=\{x\in M:G_x\text{ is conjugate to }H\}\), where \(G_x\) is the stabilizer of \(x\). Each connected component of \(M_{(H)}/G\), when nonempty, is a smooth stratum of the quotient \(M/G\). The quotient is singular at orbit types for which the local orbit dimension or isotropy representation differs from that of the principal orbit type; the collection of strata forms the orbit-type stratification.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A proper nonfree group quotient decomposes into smooth pieces indexed by conjugacy classes of stabilizers; nonprincipal pieces constitute its singular strata.
assumptions_latex: \(M\) is a smooth manifold.
\(G\) is a Lie group acting smoothly and properly on \(M\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(M/G\) is partitioned into orbit-type strata given by connected components of \(M_{(H)}/G\).

notation.meaning: Subset having stabilizer conjugate to H

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition role fits the leaf and the core orbit-type stratification claim is plausible, but no citation or inspectable locator supports the proper-action hypotheses, smoothness of the strata, or the characterization of singular orbit types.

children.title: Regular-to-Singular Transition Boundary
children.top_down_role: Regimes where smooth quotient-manifold descriptions cease to apply.

knowledge_statements.title: Regular-to-Singular Transition Boundary
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary where the principal quotient-manifold model loses regularity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let a Lie group \(G\) act smoothly and properly on \(M\), and let \(M_{\mathrm{pr}}\) be its open dense principal orbit-type subset. The regular quotient region is \(M_{\mathrm{pr}}/G\). Its transition boundary in \(M/G\) is \(\partial(M_{\mathrm{pr}}/G)=\overline{M_{\mathrm{pr}}/G}\setminus(M_{\mathrm{pr}}/G)\). Approaching this boundary, the stabilizer type ceases to be principal; consequently the orbit dimension, quotient dimension, or local slice representation may change. A single fixed-dimensional quotient-manifold chart and its associated horizontal-space construction therefore need not extend smoothly across the boundary.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The regular region ends where stabilizer type changes; quotient dimension or local geometry may then change, invalidating one smooth quotient-manifold model.
assumptions_latex: \(G\) acts smoothly and properly on \(M\).
The principal orbit-type theorem applies.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A fixed-dimensional smooth quotient model is generally valid only on \(M_{\mathrm{pr}}/G\), not across \(\partial(M_{\mathrm{pr}}/G)\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure-boundary role fits, but the boundary identity and the claimed failure of fixed-dimensional quotient charts require a precise principal-orbit-type or slice-theorem source. The current source inventory supplies none.

knowledge_statements.title: Cartesian Product Geometry
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Canonical Riemannian geometry on a finite product of manifolds.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \((M_i,g_i)\), for \(i=1,\ldots,k\), be Riemannian manifolds and set \(M=\prod_{i=1}^k M_i\). At \(x=(x_1,\ldots,x_k)\), identify \(T_xM=\prod_{i=1}^kT_{x_i}M_i\) and define the product metric by \(g_x(\xi,\eta)=\sum_{i=1}^k(g_i)_{x_i}(\xi_i,\eta_i)\). Its Levi-Civita connection acts componentwise. Hence geodesics and exponential maps are componentwise, and the induced distance satisfies \(d_M(x,y)^2=\sum_{i=1}^k d_{M_i}(x_i,y_i)^2\) whenever the component distances are finite.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A finite product carries the sum metric; tangent vectors, connections, geodesics, exponential maps, and squared distances decompose componentwise.
assumptions_latex: Each \((M_i,g_i)\) is a Riemannian manifold.
The product contains finitely many factors.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((M,g)\) has componentwise Riemannian geometry and \(d_M^2=\sum_i d_{M_i}^2\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition role fits and the finite-product formulas are standard, including the componentwise connection and distance formula when all relevant points lie in connected components. No cited source with a relevant locator is supplied.

knowledge_statements.title: Block-Separable Manifold Structure
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Differential decomposition for objectives on product manifolds.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(M=\prod_{i=1}^k M_i\) carry the product metric, and let \(f:M\to\mathbb{R}\) be smooth. Writing \(x=(x_1,\ldots,x_k)\), the Riemannian gradient is the block vector \(\operatorname{grad}f(x)=(\operatorname{grad}_1f(x),\ldots,\operatorname{grad}_kf(x))\), uniquely characterized by \((g_i)_{x_i}(\operatorname{grad}_if(x),\xi_i)=D_if(x)[\xi_i]\). If \(f(x)=\sum_{i=1}^k f_i(x_i)\), then each gradient block depends only on \(x_i\), and the Riemannian Hessian is block diagonal with diagonal blocks \(\operatorname{Hess}f_i(x_i)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: On a product manifold the gradient splits into blocks; for a sum of factorwise objectives, each block is independent and the Hessian is block diagonal.
assumptions_latex: \(M\) has the Cartesian product metric.
\(f\) is smooth.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Factorwise separability of \(f\) implies independent gradient blocks and a block-diagonal Riemannian Hessian.

notation.meaning: Differential with respect to factor i
Riemannian gradient block on factor i

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The property role fits, and the gradient and Hessian decomposition is mathematically plausible under the product metric and factorwise separability. It lacks an authoritative, specifically located source.

children.title: Redundant Factor Representations
children.top_down_role: Multiple factor tuples representing the same underlying object.

knowledge_statements.title: Redundant Factor Representations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Nonunique low-rank matrix factorization under invertible gauge transformations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix \(r\geq1\) and define \(\pi(U,V)=UV^{\mathsf T}\) for full-column-rank matrices \(U\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times r}\) and \(V\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times r}\). For every \(Q\in\mathrm{GL}(r)\), \(\pi(UQ,VQ^{-\mathsf T})=UV^{\mathsf T}\). Conversely, if \(U,V,\widetilde U,\widetilde V\) have full column rank and \(UV^{\mathsf T}=\widetilde U\widetilde V^{\mathsf T}\), then a unique \(Q\in\mathrm{GL}(r)\) satisfies \(\widetilde U=UQ\) and \(\widetilde V=VQ^{-\mathsf T}\). Thus a rank-\(r\) matrix is represented by an entire gauge orbit of factor pairs.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A full-rank factor pair representing a rank-r matrix is nonunique: all equivalent pairs are related by an invertible change of latent basis.
assumptions_latex: \(U,V,\widetilde U,\widetilde V\) have \(r\) linearly independent columns.
The represented matrices have rank \(r\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(UV^{\mathsf T}=\widetilde U\widetilde V^{\mathsf T}\) exactly when \((\widetilde U,\widetilde V)=(UQ,VQ^{-\mathsf T})\) for a unique \(Q\in\mathrm{GL}(r)\).

notation.meaning: Group of invertible r-by-r real matrices

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The representation role exactly fits the leaf, and the stated GL(r) equivalence is standard for full-column-rank factors. No source or locator supports the converse and uniqueness claim.

children.title: Gauge Symmetry Orbits
children.top_down_role: Equivalence classes induced by transformations of redundant factors.

knowledge_statements.title: Gauge Symmetry Orbits
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Orbits of a representation-preserving gauge-group action.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let a group \(G\) act smoothly on a parameter manifold \(P\), and let \(\pi:P\to X\) satisfy \(\pi(g\cdot p)=\pi(p)\) for every \(g\in G\) and \(p\in P\). The gauge-symmetry orbit through \(p\) is \(G\cdot p=\{g\cdot p:g\in G\}\). Its tangent space is the vertical space \(\mathcal V_p=T_p(G\cdot p)\), which is contained in \(\ker D\pi(p)\). If every fiber of \(\pi\) is one orbit, then the represented objects are identified with the orbit space \(P/G\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Gauge transformations move parameters without changing the represented object; their orbit is an equivalence class, and its tangent directions are representation-null directions.
assumptions_latex: \(G\) acts smoothly on \(P\).
\(\pi\) is invariant under the action.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(G\cdot p\subseteq\pi^{-1}(\pi(p))\) and \(T_p(G\cdot p)\subseteq\ker D\pi(p)\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition role fits, but X is not declared a smooth manifold and π is not assumed differentiable even though Dπ(p) and its kernel are used. A precise quotient-action source and corrected smoothness assumptions are required.

children.title: Gauge Identifiability Boundary
children.top_down_role: Limits on recovering unique factors from an invariant representation.

knowledge_statements.title: Gauge Identifiability Boundary
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary between locally identifiable quotient parameters and additional degeneracy.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G\) act on \(P\), let \(\pi:P\to X\) be invariant, and write \(\mathcal V_p=T_p(G\cdot p)\). Local identifiability modulo gauge at \(p\) requires \(\ker D\pi(p)=\mathcal V_p\) and locally constant orbit dimension. The gauge-identifiability boundary consists of points where either \(\ker D\pi(p)\supsetneq\mathcal V_p\) or the stabilizer dimension changes. At such points there are infinitesimal ambiguities not generated by the declared gauge action, or the quotient dimension changes, so a regular local quotient parametrization cannot be inferred from the gauge model.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Local identification modulo gauge fails when the representation has extra null directions or when stabilizer dimension changes, destroying a regular quotient parametrization.
assumptions_latex: \(G\) acts smoothly on \(P\).
\(\pi\) is smooth and gauge invariant.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Regular local identification modulo \(G\) fails when \(\ker D\pi(p)\neq\mathcal V_p\) or orbit dimension is not locally constant.

notation.meaning: Tangent space to the gauge orbit

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure-boundary role fits, but kernel equality and locally constant orbit dimension alone do not establish a regular local quotient parametrization without additional constant-rank, fiber, and group-action regularity hypotheses. A precise source is required to determine the valid criterion.

knowledge_statements.title: Rank-Stratification Boundary
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Loss of fixed-rank manifold structure at lower-rank limits.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For integers \(0<r\leq\min(m,n)\), the set \(\mathcal M_r=\{X\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}:\operatorname{rank}X=r\}\) is a smooth embedded manifold of dimension \(r(m+n-r)\). Its closure is \(\overline{\mathcal M_r}=\{X:\operatorname{rank}X\leq r\}\), and its boundary is \(\bigcup_{s=0}^{r-1}\mathcal M_s\). Along a sequence in \(\mathcal M_r\) approaching rank \(s<r\), at least \(r-s\) positive singular values tend to zero. The fixed-rank tangent-space model therefore does not extend as a constant-dimensional manifold model through the limit.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Fixed-rank matrices form a smooth manifold, but its boundary contains lower-rank strata where singular values vanish and the manifold dimension changes.
assumptions_latex: Matrices are real and finite dimensional.
\(0<r\leq\min(m,n)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\partial\mathcal M_r=\bigcup_{s<r}\mathcal M_s\), and fixed-rank smooth geometry fails across this boundary.

notation.meaning: Set of matrices of rank exactly r

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure-boundary role fits, but the displayed boundary formula is false for the ordinary topological boundary in the ambient matrix space: that boundary contains the rank-r stratum as well. The lower-rank union is the relative frontier of the rank-r stratum in its closure. No source is supplied to resolve and support the intended formulation.

children.title: Riemannian Distance
children.top_down_role: Global distance structure relevant to manifold optimization.

knowledge_statements.title: Riemannian Distance
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Intrinsic length distance induced by a Riemannian metric.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \((M,g)\) be a connected Riemannian manifold. For a piecewise continuously differentiable curve \(\gamma:[0,1]\to M\), define its length by \(L_g(\gamma)=\int_0^1\sqrt{g_{\gamma(t)}(\dot\gamma(t),\dot\gamma(t))}\,dt\). The Riemannian distance between \(x,y\in M\) is \(d_g(x,y)=\inf_{\gamma}L_g(\gamma)\), where the infimum ranges over all such curves satisfying \(\gamma(0)=x\) and \(\gamma(1)=y\). This distance is finite and induces the original manifold topology.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Riemannian distance is the infimum of metric lengths of piecewise smooth curves joining two points, and it induces the manifold topology.
assumptions_latex: \((M,g)\) is a connected Riemannian manifold.
Admissible curves are piecewise continuously differentiable.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(d_g(x,y)=\inf_{\gamma(0)=x,\,\gamma(1)=y}L_g(\gamma)\) defines the intrinsic metric on \(M\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition role fits and the intrinsic-distance statement is standard for a connected Riemannian manifold, but no authoritative section, theorem, definition, or page locator is cited.

children.title: Exponential Maps
children.top_down_role: Tangent-to-manifold mappings based on geodesic geometry.

knowledge_statements.title: Exponential Maps
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Endpoint map of geodesics with prescribed initial velocity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \((M,g)\) be a Riemannian manifold and \(x\in M\). For every \(v\in T_xM\) whose maximal geodesic \(\gamma_v\) with \(\gamma_v(0)=x\) and \(\dot\gamma_v(0)=v\) is defined at time \(1\), define \(\operatorname{Exp}_x(v)=\gamma_v(1)\). Its domain is an open star-shaped neighborhood of \(0_x\), and \(D\operatorname{Exp}_x(0_x)=\operatorname{id}_{T_xM}\). Consequently, \(\operatorname{Exp}_x\) is a diffeomorphism from some neighborhood of \(0_x\) onto a normal neighborhood of \(x\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The exponential map sends an initial tangent velocity to its geodesic endpoint at time one and is locally invertible near the zero vector.
assumptions_latex: \((M,g)\) is a Riemannian manifold.
The selected geodesic exists through time \(1\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{Exp}_x(v)=\gamma_v(1)\) and \(D\operatorname{Exp}_x(0_x)=\operatorname{id}_{T_xM}\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition role fits and the domain, derivative, and local-diffeomorphism claims are standard, but they are unsupported by any cited source with a specific locator.

children.title: Logarithmic Maps
children.top_down_role: Local manifold-to-tangent inverse interfaces for geodesic displacement.

knowledge_statements.title: Logarithmic Maps
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Local inverse of the exponential map on a normal neighborhood.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \((M,g)\) be a Riemannian manifold, let \(x\in M\), and let \(U\) be a normal neighborhood of \(x\) on which \(\operatorname{Exp}_x:V\to U\) is a diffeomorphism from an open set \(V\subset T_xM\). The logarithmic map based at \(x\) is \(\operatorname{Log}_x:U\to V\), defined by \(\operatorname{Log}_x(y)=\operatorname{Exp}_x^{-1}(y)\). It is the initial velocity of the unique radial geodesic from \(x\) to \(y\), and satisfies \(\lVert\operatorname{Log}_x(y)\rVert_x=d_g(x,y)\) within this normal neighborhood.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: On a normal neighborhood, the logarithmic map is the inverse exponential map and returns the initial velocity of the unique minimizing radial geodesic.
assumptions_latex: \(U\) is a normal neighborhood of \(x\).
\(y\in U\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{Log}_x(y)=\operatorname{Exp}_x^{-1}(y)\) and \(\lVert\operatorname{Log}_x(y)\rVert_x=d_g(x,y)\).

notation.meaning: Local Riemannian logarithmic map at x

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition role fits and the local inverse statement is plausible under the intended normal-neighborhood convention. A source is needed to support that convention and the minimizing-distance identity.

children.title: Geodesic Families
children.top_down_role: Geodesic curves used to describe intrinsic manifold motion.

knowledge_statements.title: Geodesic Families
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Smooth families generated by the geodesic flow.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \((M,g)\) be a Riemannian manifold and let \(D\subset TM\times\mathbb R\) be the maximal domain of the geodesic flow. A geodesic family is the smooth map \(\Gamma:D\to M\) such that, for every \((x,v)\in TM\), the curve \(t\mapsto\Gamma(x,v,t)\) on its maximal interval satisfies \(\nabla_{\dot\gamma}\dot\gamma=0\), \(\Gamma(x,v,0)=x\), and \(\partial_t\Gamma(x,v,0)=v\). Uniqueness of the geodesic initial-value problem makes this family well defined, and whenever time \(1\) belongs to the domain, \(\Gamma(x,v,1)=\operatorname{Exp}_x(v)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The geodesic flow smoothly assigns to each initial point and velocity its unique maximal geodesic; its time-one endpoint is the exponential map.
assumptions_latex: \((M,g)\) is a smooth Riemannian manifold.
\(D\) is the maximal existence domain of the geodesic equation.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\Gamma\) smoothly parametrizes all maximal geodesics by their initial data in \(TM\).

notation.meaning: Geodesic family or geodesic flow projected to M

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition role fits the leaf, and the projected geodesic-flow formulation is plausible. No source with a specific locator supports smooth dependence on initial data or the maximal-domain statement.

children.title: Geodesic Completeness
children.top_down_role: Global continuation regimes for geodesic curves.

knowledge_statements.title: Geodesic Completeness
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Metric and geodesic completeness for connected finite-dimensional Riemannian manifolds.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A connected Riemannian manifold \((M,g)\) is geodesically complete if every maximal geodesic \(\gamma:(a,b)\to M\) extends to a geodesic defined on all of \(\mathbb R\). Equivalently, for every \(p\in M\), the exponential map \(\exp_p\) is defined on all of \(T_pM\). By the Hopf–Rinow theorem, these conditions are equivalent to completeness of the metric space \((M,d_g)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A connected Riemannian manifold is complete when every geodesic exists for all time; equivalently, every exponential map has full tangent-space domain and the induced metric space is complete.
assumptions_latex: \((M,g)\) is a connected finite-dimensional Riemannian manifold.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(M\text{ is geodesically complete}\iff \operatorname{dom}(\exp_p)=T_pM\ \forall p\in M\iff (M,d_g)\text{ is complete}.\)

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition and Hopf–Rinow equivalences are mathematically standard and fit the leaf, but no source or inspectable locator supports them. The supplied inventory is unrelated.

children.title: Geodesic Reachability
children.top_down_role: Connectivity of manifold points through admissible geodesic segments.

knowledge_statements.title: Geodesic Reachability
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Hopf–Rinow reachability by globally minimizing geodesics.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \((M,g)\) be connected and complete. For every \(p,q\in M\), there exists \(v\in T_pM\) such that \(q=\exp_p(v)\) and the radial geodesic \(\gamma(t)=\exp_p(tv)\), \(0\le t\le1\), minimizes length between its endpoints. Consequently, \(L(\gamma)=\lVert v\rVert_g=d_g(p,q)\), so every point is reachable from every other point by a minimizing geodesic.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: On a connected complete Riemannian manifold, every pair of points is joined by a length-minimizing geodesic obtained from the exponential map.
assumptions_latex: \((M,g)\) is connected and complete.
\(p,q\in M\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\exists v\in T_pM:\ q=\exp_p(v),\quad L(t\mapsto\exp_p(tv))=\lVert v\rVert_g=d_g(p,q).\)

notation.meaning: Riemannian length of the curve γ

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The stated minimizing-geodesic reachability theorem is a standard Hopf–Rinow consequence and fits the container, but it has no cited authoritative source or theorem/section locator.

children.title: Curvature Regimes
children.top_down_role: Curvature classifications relevant to local or global optimization geometry.

knowledge_statements.title: Curvature Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Pointwise sectional-curvature regimes relevant to comparison geometry.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a Riemannian manifold \((M,g)\) and constants \(\kappa_-\le\kappa_+\), the two-sided curvature regime \(\kappa_-\le\sec_M\le\kappa_+\) means that every point \(p\in M\) and every two-dimensional subspace \(\sigma\subset T_pM\) satisfy \(\kappa_-\le\sec_p(\sigma)\le\kappa_+\). The special regimes \(\sec_M\le0\), \(\sec_M=0\), and \(\sec_M\ge0\) are respectively nonpositive, flat, and nonnegative sectional curvature.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A curvature regime imposes uniform lower and upper bounds on sectional curvature over every tangent two-plane; sign regimes arise by comparison with zero.
assumptions_latex: \((M,g)\) is a Riemannian manifold.
\(\kappa_-,\kappa_+\in\mathbb R\) with \(\kappa_-\le\kappa_+\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\kappa_-\le\sec_M\le\kappa_+\iff \kappa_-\le\sec_p(\sigma)\le\kappa_+\quad\forall p\in M,\ \forall\sigma\in\operatorname{Gr}_2(T_pM).\)

notation.meaning: sectional curvature of the tangent two-plane σ at p
set of two-dimensional linear subspaces of the tangent space

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The sectional-curvature regimes are precise and the condition kind fits the leaf, but the record supplies no supporting source or locator.

children.title: Injectivity Radius
children.top_down_role: Local scale governing uniqueness of exponential-map representations.

knowledge_statements.title: Injectivity Radius
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Pointwise and global injectivity radii of the exponential map.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(p\in M\), the injectivity radius is \[\operatorname{inj}(p):=\sup\{r>0:\exp_p|_{B(0,r)}:B(0,r)\subset T_pM\to M\text{ is a diffeomorphism onto its image}\}.\] The global injectivity radius is \(\operatorname{inj}(M):=\inf_{p\in M}\operatorname{inj}(p)\). If \(0<r<\operatorname{inj}(p)\), each point of \(\exp_p(B(0,r))\) has a unique radial geodesic from \(p\), and this geodesic minimizes distance.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The injectivity radius is the largest tangent-ball radius on which the exponential map is one-to-one and nonsingular; the global radius is the infimum over base points.
assumptions_latex: \((M,g)\) is a Riemannian manifold.
\(p\in M\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(0<r<\operatorname{inj}(p)\Longrightarrow \exp_p|_{B(0,r)}\text{ is a diffeomorphism onto its image}.\)

notation.meaning: open radius-r ball for the norm induced by g_p

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The pointwise and global definitions are standard and locally appropriate, but the definition and its uniqueness/minimality consequence lack an authoritative citation with a specific locator.

children.title: Convexity Radius
children.top_down_role: Local scale associated with geodesically convex neighborhoods.

knowledge_statements.title: Convexity Radius
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Radius of strongly geodesically convex metric balls.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An open set \(U\subset M\) is strongly geodesically convex if every \(x,y\in U\) are joined by a unique minimizing geodesic in \(M\) whose image lies in \(U\). For \(p\in M\), define \[\operatorname{conv}(p):=\sup\{r>0:B_g(p,s)\text{ is strongly geodesically convex for every }0<s<r\}.\] The global convexity radius is \(\operatorname{conv}(M):=\inf_{p\in M}\operatorname{conv}(p)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The convexity radius at a point is the largest scale below which all centered metric balls contain a unique minimizing geodesic between every two of their points.
assumptions_latex: \((M,g)\) is a Riemannian manifold.
\(p\in M\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(0<s<\operatorname{conv}(p)\Longrightarrow B_g(p,s)\text{ is strongly geodesically convex}.\)

notation.meaning: open Riemannian metric ball centered at p

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The strong-convexity and convexity-radius definitions fit the terminal container, but no source or inspectable locator is provided.

children.title: Curvature–Radius Interactions
children.top_down_role: Structural influence of curvature on injectivity or convexity scales.

knowledge_statements.title: Curvature–Radius Interactions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A conservative local scale combining curvature and injectivity constraints.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \((M,g)\) have sectional curvature bounded above by \(K\ge0\), and define \(r_K=+\infty\) when \(K=0\) and \(r_K=\pi/(2\sqrt K)\) when \(K>0\). If \(0<r<\min\{\operatorname{inj}(M)/2,r_K\}\), then every metric ball \(B_g(p,r)\) is strongly geodesically convex. Thus positive curvature and loss of injectivity jointly limit a uniform radius on which minimizing geodesics are unique and remain inside the ball.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A uniform strongly convex neighborhood scale is bounded jointly by half the global injectivity radius and, under positive curvature, a curvature-dependent radius.
assumptions_latex: \((M,g)\) is a complete Riemannian manifold.
\(\sec_M\le K\) for some \(K\ge0\).
\(0<r<\min\{\operatorname{inj}(M)/2,r_K\}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(B_g(p,r)\text{ is strongly geodesically convex for every }p\in M.\)

notation.meaning: curvature-controlled radius, infinite for K=0 and π/(2√K) for K>0

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The claim is relevant to curvature–radius interactions, but the uniform strong-convexity bound, including the factors 1/2 and π/(2√K), requires direct verification against a theorem with matching completeness and curvature hypotheses.

children.title: Cut-Locus Geometry
children.top_down_role: Geometric structure where minimizing-geodesic behavior changes.

knowledge_statements.title: Cut-Locus Geometry
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Cut locus defined by terminal minimizing radial geodesics.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix \(p\in M\). For a unit vector \(v\in T_pM\), let \(c(v):=\sup\{t>0:s\mapsto\exp_p(sv),\ 0\le s\le t,\text{ minimizes distance from }p\}\). The cut locus of \(p\) is \[\operatorname{Cut}(p):=\{\exp_p(c(v)v):\lVert v\rVert_g=1,\ c(v)<+\infty\}.\] Before the cut time, the radial geodesic is the unique minimizing geodesic from \(p\); beyond it, that radial segment is not minimizing.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The cut locus consists of endpoints where radial geodesics cease to remain uniquely minimizing; each direction has a corresponding cut time, possibly infinite.
assumptions_latex: \((M,g)\) is a complete Riemannian manifold.
\(p\in M\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(0<t<c(v)\Longrightarrow s\mapsto\exp_p(sv),\ 0\le s\le t,\text{ is uniquely minimizing}.\)

notation.meaning: cut time in the unit tangent direction v

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The cut-time definition is standard but uncited. The plain statement also suggests every cut point is where uniqueness fails, whereas a cut point may arise through conjugacy while its minimizing geodesic remains unique; an authoritative source is needed to settle and restate the exact boundary behavior.

children.title: Nonunique Minimizing Geodesics
children.top_down_role: Regions admitting multiple minimizing geodesic connections.

knowledge_statements.title: Nonunique Minimizing Geodesics
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Multiplicity branch of the cut-locus alternative.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \((M,g)\) be complete and \(q\in\operatorname{Cut}(p)\). Then either at least two distinct minimizing geodesics join \(p\) to \(q\), or \(q\) is conjugate to \(p\) along a minimizing geodesic. In the first case there exist distinct \(v,w\in T_pM\) with \(\lVert v\rVert_g=\lVert w\rVert_g=d_g(p,q)\) and \(\exp_p(v)=\exp_p(w)=q\). Hence the inverse logarithm at \(p\) is set-valued at \(q\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At a cut point, minimizing geodesics either become nonunique or encounter conjugacy; in the nonunique case, distinct tangent vectors exponentiate to the same endpoint.
assumptions_latex: \((M,g)\) is complete.
\(p\in M\) and \(q\in\operatorname{Cut}(p)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\#\{\text{minimizing geodesics from }p\text{ to }q\}\ge2\quad\text{or}\quad q\text{ is conjugate to }p.\)

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The cut-point alternative is a theorem rather than merely a generic property. It also lacks a source locator supporting the precise alternative and the claimed logarithm behavior.

children.title: Distance-Smoothness Failure Boundary
children.top_down_role: Loss of smooth distance-based representations near cut loci.

knowledge_statements.title: Distance-Smoothness Failure Boundary
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Smoothness boundary for distance and squared-distance functions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix \(p\) in a complete Riemannian manifold. The function \(q\mapsto d_g(p,q)\) is smooth on \(M\setminus(\{p\}\cup\operatorname{Cut}(p))\), while \(q\mapsto \tfrac12d_g(p,q)^2\) is smooth on \(M\setminus\operatorname{Cut}(p)\). If \(q\in\operatorname{Cut}(p)\) admits two distinct minimizing geodesics from \(p\), then \(d_g(p,\cdot)\) and \(\tfrac12d_g(p,\cdot)^2\) are not differentiable at \(q\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Distance is smooth away from its base point and cut locus, while squared distance is smooth away from the cut locus; multiple minimizers force nondifferentiability.
assumptions_latex: \((M,g)\) is complete.
\(p\in M\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(q\notin\{p\}\cup\operatorname{Cut}(p)\Longrightarrow d_g(p,\cdot)\text{ is smooth near }q;\) multiplicity at a cut point implies nondifferentiability.

notation.meaning: distance from the fixed point p

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The smoothness domains and nondifferentiability under multiple minimizers fit the failure-boundary leaf, but these nontrivial claims have no cited theorem, section, or page.

children.top_down_role: First- and second-order calculus together with the local approximation and transport mechanisms used by algorithms.

children.title: Manifold Differentials
children.top_down_role: Intrinsic first-order variation of smooth manifold maps.

knowledge_statements.title: Manifold Differentials
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Intrinsic differential of a smooth map between manifolds.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F:M\to N\) be smooth and \(p\in M\). The differential of \(F\) at \(p\) is the linear map \(dF_p:T_pM\to T_{F(p)}N\) defined by \[dF_p(v):=(F\circ\gamma)'(0),\] where \(\gamma:(-\varepsilon,\varepsilon)\to M\) is any smooth curve satisfying \(\gamma(0)=p\) and \(\gamma'(0)=v\). This value is independent of the representing curve.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The differential sends a tangent velocity at the source to the velocity of its image under the map, independently of the curve representing that velocity.
assumptions_latex: \(M,N\) are smooth manifolds.
\(F:M\to N\) is smooth and \(p\in M\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(dF_p:T_pM\to T_{F(p)}N\text{ is a well-defined linear map}.\)

notation.meaning: tangent space of M at p

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The intrinsic differential is correctly presented as a definition and fits the leaf, but no authoritative textbook section or definition locator is supplied.

children.title: Tangent-Space Derivatives
children.top_down_role: Derivative mappings between source plus target tangent spaces.

knowledge_statements.title: Tangent-Space Derivatives
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Directional derivative represented as a tangent-space covector.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f:M\to\mathbb R\) be smooth. At \(p\in M\), its tangent-space derivative is the covector \(df_p\in T_p^*M\) satisfying \[df_p[v]=\left.\frac{d}{dt}f(\gamma(t))\right|_{t=0}\] for every \(v\in T_pM\) and every smooth curve \(\gamma\) with \(\gamma(0)=p\) and \(\gamma'(0)=v\). If \(M\) has metric \(g\), the Riemannian gradient is uniquely determined by \(df_p[v]=g_p(\operatorname{grad}f(p),v)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A scalar function's derivative is a covector on the tangent space; a Riemannian metric uniquely represents that covector by the gradient vector.
assumptions_latex: \(M\) is a smooth manifold and \(f:M\to\mathbb R\) is smooth.
\(p\in M\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(df_p\in T_p^*M;\quad df_p[v]=g_p(\operatorname{grad}f(p),v)\text{ when }g\text{ is specified}.\)

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The covector representation and metric duality with the Riemannian gradient fit the representation container, but neither claim has an inspectable citation.

children.title: Coordinate Representations of Derivatives
children.top_down_role: Local-coordinate realizations of intrinsic derivative objects.

knowledge_statements.title: Coordinate Representations of Derivatives
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Chart-matrix representation of the intrinsic differential.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F:M\to N\) be smooth, let \(x=(x^1,\ldots,x^m)\) be a chart near \(p\), and let \(y=(y^1,\ldots,y^n)\) be a chart near \(F(p)\). Relative to the coordinate tangent bases, \(dF_p\) is represented by the Jacobian \[J_{y\circ F\circ x^{-1}}(x(p))=\left[\frac{\partial(y^\alpha\circ F)}{\partial x^i}(p)\right]_{\alpha,i}.\] Under new charts, this matrix changes by left and right multiplication with the corresponding transition-map Jacobians, while \(dF_p\) itself is chart independent.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: In source and target charts, the intrinsic differential is represented by the ordinary Jacobian; coordinate changes transform its matrix but not the underlying linear map.
assumptions_latex: \(F:M\to N\) is smooth.
\(x\) and \(y\) are charts at \(p\) and \(F(p)\), respectively.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \([dF_p]_{x,y}=J_{y\circ F\circ x^{-1}}(x(p)).\)

notation.meaning: matrix of the differential in the coordinate tangent bases
ordinary Jacobian matrix of a coordinate map h

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The Jacobian representation of the intrinsic differential is standard and appropriate, but the record provides no source or specific locator for the formula and chart-change claim.

children.title: Riemannian Metric Structure
children.top_down_role: Inner-product geometry assigned across tangent spaces.

knowledge_statements.title: Riemannian Metric Structure
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Smooth finite-dimensional Riemannian metric used to identify tangent vectors and covectors.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(M\) be a smooth manifold. A Riemannian metric on \(M\) is a family \(g=(g_x)_{x\in M}\) such that each \(g_x:T_xM\times T_xM\to\mathbb R\) is a symmetric positive-definite bilinear form and, for all smooth vector fields \(X,Y\), the function \(x\mapsto g_x(X_x,Y_x)\) is smooth. It induces the norm \(\|\xi\|_x=\sqrt{g_x(\xi,\xi)}\) and the musical isomorphism \(g_x^\flat:T_xM\to T_x^*M\), defined by \(g_x^\flat(\xi)[\eta]=g_x(\xi,\eta)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A Riemannian metric is a smoothly varying inner product on tangent spaces; it induces tangent norms and identifies tangent vectors with cotangent vectors.
assumptions_latex: \(M\) is a smooth finite-dimensional manifold.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(g_x^\flat:T_xM\to T_x^*M\) is a linear isomorphism for every \(x\in M\).

notation.meaning: tangent space of the manifold at x

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition, induced norm, and finite-dimensional musical isomorphism are mathematically appropriate, but no source or inspectable locator is supplied.

children.title: Riemannian Gradient Construction
children.top_down_role: Metric-dependent representation of first-order objective variation.

knowledge_statements.title: Riemannian Gradient Construction
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Metric representation of the differential of a smooth objective.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \((M,g)\) be a Riemannian manifold and let \(f:M\to\mathbb R\) be smooth. For each \(x\in M\), the Riemannian gradient \(\operatorname{grad}f(x)\in T_xM\) is the unique tangent vector satisfying \[g_x\bigl(\operatorname{grad}f(x),\xi\bigr)=\mathrm df(x)[\xi]\qquad\text{for every }\xi\in T_xM.\] Equivalently, \(\operatorname{grad}f(x)=(g_x^\flat)^{-1}(\mathrm df(x))\). Thus the differential is metric-independent, whereas its representing tangent vector is determined by \(g\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The Riemannian gradient is the unique tangent vector whose metric inner product with every direction equals the directional derivative.
assumptions_latex: \((M,g)\) is a smooth finite-dimensional Riemannian manifold.
\(f:M\to\mathbb R\) is smooth.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{grad}f(x)=(g_x^\flat)^{-1}(\mathrm df(x))\) exists uniquely for every \(x\in M\).

notation.meaning: Riemannian gradient of f at x

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The metric representation of the differential correctly constructs the Riemannian gradient and fits the leaf, but it has no supporting citation or locator.

children.title: Gradient Dependence on Metric Choice
children.top_down_role: How alternative metrics alter gradient representations or conditioning.

knowledge_statements.title: Gradient Dependence on Metric Choice
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Transformation law for gradients under two Riemannian metrics.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(g\) and \(h\) be Riemannian metrics on \(M\). For each \(x\in M\), let \(A_x:T_xM\to T_xM\) be the unique \(g_x\)-self-adjoint positive-definite operator satisfying \(h_x(u,v)=g_x(A_xu,v)\) for all \(u,v\in T_xM\). Then every smooth \(f:M\to\mathbb R\) satisfies \[\operatorname{grad}_{h}f(x)=A_x^{-1}\operatorname{grad}_{g}f(x).\] Consequently, changing the metric generally changes the gradient vector and steepest-descent direction, while leaving \(\mathrm df(x)\) and the critical-point condition \(\mathrm df(x)=0\) unchanged.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If one metric equals another through a positive-definite operator, their gradients differ by the inverse operator; critical points remain unchanged.
assumptions_latex: \(g\) and \(h\) are Riemannian metrics on the same smooth manifold \(M\).
\(f:M\to\mathbb R\) is smooth.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{grad}_{h}f(x)=A_x^{-1}\operatorname{grad}_{g}f(x)\), and \(\operatorname{grad}_{h}f(x)=0\iff\operatorname{grad}_{g}f(x)=0\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The metric-change operator and inverse transformation law are mathematically plausible and locally appropriate, but the nontrivial formula lacks cited evidence and an inspectable locator.

knowledge_statements.title: Embedded Gradient Calculus
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Gradient formula for an embedded submanifold with its induced metric.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(M\) be a smooth embedded submanifold of a Euclidean space \(E\), equipped with the induced metric, and let \(f:M\to\mathbb R\) admit a smooth extension \(\bar f\) to a neighborhood of \(M\). If \(P_x:E\to T_xM\) is the orthogonal projector, then \[\operatorname{grad}f(x)=P_x\nabla\bar f(x).\] This expression is independent of the chosen extension because any two extensions have ambient gradients whose difference is orthogonal to \(T_xM\). Equivalently, \(\langle\operatorname{grad}f(x),\xi\rangle=\mathrm df(x)[\xi]\) for every \(\xi\in T_xM\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: On an embedded manifold with induced metric, project the ambient Euclidean gradient orthogonally onto the tangent space.
assumptions_latex: \(M\subset E\) is a smooth embedded submanifold with the induced Euclidean metric.
\(\bar f\) is a smooth local extension of \(f\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{grad}f(x)=P_x\nabla\bar f(x)\), independently of the extension.

notation.meaning: orthogonal projection from the ambient space onto the tangent space

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The projected ambient-gradient representation is correct under the stated induced-metric and extension assumptions, but no source or locator supports it.

knowledge_statements.title: Quotient Gradient Calculus
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Horizontal-lift representation of gradients on a Riemannian quotient.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\pi:\bar M\to M=\bar M/G\) be a Riemannian quotient map, with horizontal space \(\mathcal H_{\bar x}\) orthogonal to the vertical space \(\ker\mathrm D\pi(\bar x)\). For smooth \(f:M\to\mathbb R\), define the invariant lift \(\bar f=f\circ\pi\). Then \(\operatorname{grad}\bar f(\bar x)\) is horizontal and is the unique horizontal lift of the quotient gradient: \[\mathrm D\pi(\bar x)[\operatorname{grad}\bar f(\bar x)]=\operatorname{grad}f(\pi(\bar x)).\] More generally, if an ambient representative is first obtained, its horizontal projection represents the quotient gradient.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a Riemannian quotient, the gradient of the invariant lifted objective is horizontal and projects to the quotient gradient.
assumptions_latex: \(\pi:\bar M\to M\) is a Riemannian submersion defining a smooth quotient.
\(f:M\to\mathbb R\) is smooth.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{grad}\bar f(\bar x)\in\mathcal H_{\bar x}\) and \(\mathrm D\pi(\bar x)[\operatorname{grad}\bar f(\bar x)]=\operatorname{grad}f(\pi(\bar x))\).

notation.meaning: horizontal tangent space at the representative point
invariant lift of the quotient objective

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The horizontal-lift formula is appropriate for a Riemannian submersion, but no source is cited; the final claim about projecting an ambient representative also requires its ambient embedding and projection assumptions to be sourced precisely.

children.title: Riemannian Connections
children.top_down_role: Metric-compatible connection structures used in Riemannian calculus.

knowledge_statements.title: Riemannian Connections
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Metric-compatible affine connections used in Riemannian calculus.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \((M,g)\) be a Riemannian manifold. A Riemannian, or metric-compatible, connection is an affine connection \(
abla\) satisfying \[X igl(g(Y,Z) igr)=g(
abla_XY,Z)+g(Y,
abla_XZ)\] for every smooth vector field \(X,Y,Z\). Equivalently, parallel transport defined by \(
abla\) preserves the metric inner product along every smooth curve. Metric compatibility alone does not generally determine the connection uniquely; uniqueness follows after imposing vanishing torsion.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A Riemannian connection is an affine connection that preserves the metric under covariant differentiation and parallel transport.
assumptions_latex: \((M,g)\) is a smooth Riemannian manifold.
\(\nabla\) is an affine connection on \(M\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\nabla g=0\), equivalently its parallel transport preserves \(g\).

smooth function obtained by pairing vector fields under the metric

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Metric compatibility and its parallel-transport interpretation are mathematically appropriate, but terminology for “Riemannian connection” varies and must be anchored to a specific source with a locator.

children.title: Torsion-Free Metric Compatibility
children.top_down_role: Structural regime selecting the standard Riemannian connection.

knowledge_statements.title: Torsion-Free Metric Compatibility
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Fundamental theorem selecting the Levi-Civita connection.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \((M,g)\) be a smooth finite-dimensional Riemannian manifold. There exists a unique affine connection \(
abla\) such that it is metric-compatible and torsion-free: \[X igl(g(Y,Z) igr)=g(
abla_XY,Z)+g(Y,
abla_XZ),\qquad 
abla_XY-
abla_YX=[X,Y]\] for all smooth vector fields \(X,Y,Z\). This unique connection is the Levi-Civita connection of \(g\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every Riemannian metric determines exactly one affine connection that both preserves the metric and has zero torsion: the Levi-Civita connection.
assumptions_latex: \((M,g)\) is a smooth finite-dimensional Riemannian manifold.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex:
There exists a unique affine connection \(
abla\) with \(
