knowledge_statements.title: Irregular-Constraint Boundary
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary where a constraint presentation ceases to define the intrinsic geometry reliably.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a level-set model \(\mathcal F=h^{-1}(0)\), the regular interface requires locally constant full row rank of \(Dh\). If this fails, \(\ker Dh(x)\) need not equal the geometric tangent space, multipliers need not exist or be unique, and Lagrangian-Hessian tests may depend on the chosen constraint representation. For example, \(h(t)=t^2\) has \(\mathcal F=\{0\}\), whose tangent space is \(\{0\}\), but \(\ker Dh(0)=\mathbb R\). Hence the Jacobian-based ambient model introduces spurious linearized directions and cannot be translated mechanically into intrinsic manifold optimality conditions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At rank-deficient constraints, the Jacobian kernel can differ from the true tangent space, so multiplier and Hessian translations may fail.
assumptions_latex: The feasible set is presented as \(h^{-1}(0)\).
No constant-rank or full-row-rank condition is imposed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Without constraint regularity, \(\ker Dh(x)\) may not represent the intrinsic tangent space.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The rank-deficient example and failure-boundary role are appropriate, but the claims concerning multiplier and Hessian representation dependence lack an inspectable source.

knowledge_statements.title: Geodesically Convex Domains
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Existence-based geodesic convexity for subsets of a Riemannian manifold.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \((\mathcal M,g)\) be a Riemannian manifold. A set \(C\subseteq\mathcal M\) is geodesically convex if, for every \(x,y\in C\), there exists a minimizing geodesic \(\gamma:[0,1]\to\mathcal M\) such that \(\gamma(0)=x\), \(\gamma(1)=y\), and \(\gamma(t)\in C\) for every \(t\in[0,1]\). It is strongly geodesically convex if this minimizing geodesic is unique and lies in \(C\). This record uses the existence convention for “geodesically convex”; requiring every connecting minimizing geodesic to remain in \(C\) is a distinct stronger convention.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A domain is geodesically convex when each pair of its points can be joined inside it by a minimizing geodesic.
assumptions_latex: \((\mathcal M,g)\) is a Riemannian manifold.
\(C\subseteq\mathcal M\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(C\) contains a minimizing geodesic segment joining every pair of its points.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The existence-based definition is coherent and explicitly distinguishes stronger conventions, but no source establishes the selected convention or terminology.

knowledge_statements.title: Geodesically Convex Objectives
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Convexity along all geodesic segments contained in the domain.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(C\) be a geodesically convex subset of a Riemannian manifold and let \(f:C\to\mathbb R\). The function \(f\) is geodesically convex on \(C\) if, for every geodesic segment \(\gamma:[0,1]\to C\),
\[f(\gamma(t))\le (1-t)f(\gamma(0))+t f(\gamma(1))\qquad\text{for all }t\in[0,1].\]
If \(f\) is differentiable and the relevant minimizing geodesic from \(x\) to \(y\) is represented by \(\gamma(t)=\operatorname{Exp}_x(t\xi)\), this implies
\[f(y)\ge f(x)+\langle\operatorname{grad}f(x),\xi\rangle_x.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A function is geodesically convex when its restriction to every admissible geodesic segment is an ordinary convex function of the segment parameter.
assumptions_latex: \(C\) is geodesically convex.
\(f:C\to\mathbb R\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f\circ\gamma\) is convex on \([0,1]\) for every geodesic segment \(\gamma\) in \(C\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition is mathematically coherent, but quantifying over every contained geodesic segment is convention-sensitive and the first-order consequence has no authoritative citation.

knowledge_statements.title: Strong Geodesic Convexity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Metric strong convexity along minimizing geodesic segments.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(C\) be geodesically convex and let \(\mu>0\). A function \(f:C\to\mathbb R\) is \(\mu\)-strongly geodesically convex if every constant-speed minimizing geodesic \(\gamma:[0,1]\to C\) satisfies
\[f(\gamma(t))\le(1-t)f(\gamma(0))+t f(\gamma(1))-\frac{\mu}{2}t(1-t)d(\gamma(0),\gamma(1))^2\]
for every \(t\in[0,1]\). When \(f\) is differentiable and \(y=\operatorname{Exp}_x(\xi)\) along such a segment, the equivalent first-order inequality is
\[f(y)\ge f(x)+\langle\operatorname{grad}f(x),\xi\rangle_x+\frac{\mu}{2}d(x,y)^2.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Strong geodesic convexity adds a uniform quadratic distance term to the ordinary convexity inequality along every minimizing geodesic.
assumptions_latex: \(C\) is geodesically convex.
Geodesics are constant-speed and minimizing.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f\circ\gamma\) obeys the displayed \(\mu\)-strong convexity inequality on every admissible geodesic.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The strong-convexity inequality is standard under the stated constant-speed minimizing-geodesic convention, but the definition and claimed first-order equivalence require an authoritative source.

children.title: Retraction Convexity
children.top_down_role: Convexity expressed through retraction-generated local parameterizations.

knowledge_statements.title: Retraction Convexity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Local convexity of retraction pullbacks on tangent-space domains.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(R\) be a retraction on a Riemannian manifold, let \(x\in\mathcal M\), and let \(U_x\subseteq T_x\mathcal M\) be convex, contain \(0_x\), and lie in the domain of \(R_x\). A function \(f\) is retraction-convex at \(x\) on \(U_x\) if the pullback \(\widehat f_x=f\circ R_x\) is convex on \(U_x\); equivalently,
\[f(R_x((1-t)\xi+t\eta))\le(1-t)f(R_x(\xi))+t f(R_x(\eta))\]
for all \(\xi,\eta\in U_x\) and \(t\in[0,1]\). Retraction convexity is relative to both the chosen retraction and tangent-space neighborhood.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Retraction convexity means that composing the objective with a chosen retraction produces an ordinary convex function on a convex tangent-space neighborhood.
assumptions_latex: \(R\) is a retraction.
\(U_x\subseteq T_x\mathcal M\) is convex and contains \(0_x\).
\(R_x\) is defined on \(U_x\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f\circ R_x\) is convex on \(U_x\).

notation.meaning: retraction restricted to the tangent space at x
retraction pullback of f at x

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Pullback convexity is a coherent definition and fits the leaf, but retraction-convexity terminology is convention-dependent and no citation is supplied.

children.title: Local Geodesic Convexity
children.top_down_role: Convex behavior restricted to suitable geodesic neighborhoods.

knowledge_statements.title: Local Geodesic Convexity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Pointwise local version of geodesic convexity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(f:\mathcal M\to\mathbb R\) and \(x\in\mathcal M\). The function \(f\) is locally geodesically convex at \(x\) if there exists a strongly geodesically convex neighborhood \(U\) of \(x\) such that, for every minimizing geodesic \(\gamma:[0,1]\to U\),
\[f(\gamma(t))\le(1-t)f(\gamma(0))+t f(\gamma(1))\qquad(t\in[0,1]).\]
It is locally geodesically convex on a set \(C\) if this property holds at every \(x\in C\), with neighborhoods allowed to depend on \(x\). No global geodesic connection between arbitrary points of \(C\) is required.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A function is locally geodesically convex when it is convex along minimizing geodesics inside some strongly geodesically convex neighborhood of each point.
assumptions_latex: \((\mathcal M,g)\) is a Riemannian manifold.
\(f:\mathcal M\to\mathbb R\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Near each designated point, \(f\) restricts to a geodesically convex function on a strongly geodesically convex neighborhood.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The pointwise local definition is coherent and matches the leaf, but its strongly geodesically convex-neighborhood convention lacks an authoritative citation.

children.title: Retraction–Geodesic Compatibility
children.top_down_role: Local regimes where retraction-based structure agrees with geodesic structure.

assumptions_latex: \((\mathcal M,g)\) is a Riemannian manifold and \(R:T\mathcal M\to\mathcal M\) is a second-order retraction.
\(f:\mathcal M\to\mathbb R\) is twice continuously differentiable near \(x\in\mathcal M\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{Hess}(f\circ R_x)(0_x)=\operatorname{Hess}f(x)\), so their quadratic convexity tests at \(x\) coincide.

notation.meaning: retraction restricted to the tangent space at x

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Second-order agreement between a retraction pullback and the exponential-map model at the base point.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A second-order retraction satisfies \(R_x(0_x)=x\), \(\mathrm D R_x(0_x)=\operatorname{id}_{T_x\mathcal M}\), and zero covariant acceleration at \(t=0\) for \(t\mapsto R_x(t\xi)\). Consequently, for every \(\xi\in T_x\mathcal M\), \[\left.\frac{\mathrm d^2}{\mathrm dt^2}f(R_x(t\xi))\right|_{t=0}=\left.\frac{\mathrm d^2}{\mathrm dt^2}f(\operatorname{Exp}_x(t\xi))\right|_{t=0}=\langle\operatorname{Hess}f(x)[\xi],\xi\rangle_x.\] Thus the pullback Hessian at the origin equals the Riemannian Hessian, although convexity away from the origin need not agree.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A second-order retraction and the exponential map give the same second-order objective model at their base point, but their finite-neighborhood convexity may differ.
knowledge_statements.title: Retraction–Geodesic Compatibility

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The property fits the compatibility leaf and is mathematically plausible, but no citation supports the precise second-order-retraction and pullback-Hessian claims. The explanatory derivation is proof text and should be removed after sourcing.

children.title: Local Convexity Breakdown
children.top_down_role: Neighborhood, curvature, plus retraction effects that prevent local convex organization.

assumptions_latex: \(R\) is a smooth retraction on a Riemannian manifold \((\mathcal M,g)\).
\(f:\mathcal M\to\mathbb R\) is twice continuously differentiable.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Positive Riemannian Hessian does not ensure convexity of \(f\circ R_x\) away from \(0_x\) when the retraction acceleration term is nonzero.

notation.meaning: retraction curve generated by a tangent vector

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Identifies the acceleration term that can destroy local retraction convexity beyond base-point agreement.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(c(t)=R_x(t\xi)\), the pullback curvature satisfies \[\frac{\mathrm d^2}{\mathrm dt^2}f(c(t))=\langle\operatorname{Hess}f(c(t))[\dot c(t)],\dot c(t)\rangle_{c(t)}+\langle\operatorname{grad}f(c(t)),\nabla_{\dot c(t)}\dot c(t)\rangle_{c(t)}.\] The second term vanishes along geodesics but generally not along retraction curves. Hence even if \(\operatorname{Hess}f\) is positive semidefinite on a neighborhood, \(f\circ R_x\) can lose convexity where the acceleration term is sufficiently negative. Second-order compatibility controls this term only at \(t=0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Retraction curves have an acceleration contribution absent from geodesics. Away from the base point, that contribution can overturn positive Riemannian curvature and destroy pullback convexity.
knowledge_statements.title: Local Convexity Breakdown

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure-boundary kind fits the leaf, and the acceleration identity is plausible, but its regularity and sign-based breakdown claim require an authoritative locator. The derivation is proof text.

assumptions_latex: \((\mathcal M,g)\) is connected, compact, and has no boundary.
\(f:\mathcal M\to\mathbb R\) is twice continuously differentiable and geodesically convex along every geodesic segment.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f\) is constant on \(\mathcal M\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Compact boundaryless-manifold obstruction for globally defined smooth geodesically convex objectives.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Geodesic convexity implies \(\operatorname{Hess}f(x)\succeq0\) for every \(x\in\mathcal M\), and therefore \(\Delta f(x)=\operatorname{tr}(\operatorname{Hess}f(x))\geq0\). On a compact manifold without boundary, \(\int_{\mathcal M}\Delta f\,\mathrm dV=0\); hence \(\Delta f=0\). Positive semidefiniteness together with zero trace gives \(\operatorname{Hess}f=0\). Since \(f\) attains a maximum and is harmonic, it is constant on connected \(\mathcal M\). Thus nonconstant globally geodesically convex smooth objectives require a restricted domain or different global geometry.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every smooth function convex along all geodesics of a connected compact boundaryless manifold is constant, obstructing nontrivial global geodesic convexity.
knowledge_statements.title: Global Geodesic-Convexity Obstructions

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The compact-manifold obstruction fits the topic and appears standard, but no source supports the exact hypotheses and conclusion. The Laplacian and maximum-principle argument is proof text.

assumptions_latex: \(C\subseteq\mathcal M\) is geodesically convex, with a selected minimizing geodesic in \(C\) between each ordered pair.
\(f:C\to\mathbb R\) is differentiable and geodesically convex.
\(x_\star\in\operatorname{int}C\) satisfies \(\operatorname{grad}f(x_\star)=0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f(y)\geq f(x_\star)\) for every \(y\in C\), so \(x_\star\) is globally optimal on \(C\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Interior stationarity as a verifiable global-optimality certificate under geodesic convexity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For any \(y\in C\), let \(\gamma:[0,1]\to C\) be the selected minimizing geodesic from \(x_\star\) to \(y\). Convexity of \(f\circ\gamma\) gives \[f(y)\geq f(x_\star)+(f\circ\gamma)'(0)=f(x_\star)+\langle\operatorname{grad}f(x_\star),\dot\gamma(0)\rangle_{x_\star}.\] The displayed gradient is zero, so \(f(y)\geq f(x_\star)\) for every feasible \(y\). The computable equality \(\operatorname{grad}f(x_\star)=0\), together with domain and objective geodesic convexity, therefore certifies global optimality.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: On a geodesically convex domain, a differentiable geodesically convex objective has no suboptimal interior stationary point; zero gradient certifies global optimality.
knowledge_statements.title: Stationarity–Global-Optimality Certificates

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Certificate is the correct kind, but no source verifies the selected-geodesic convention and support inequality used to certify global optimality. The displayed derivation is proof text.

assumptions_latex: \(C\subseteq\mathcal M\) is geodesically convex and every pair is joined by an admissible minimizing geodesic of length \(d(x,y)\).
\(f:C\to\mathbb R\) is \(\mu\)-strongly geodesically convex for some \(\mu>0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every minimizer \(x_\star\) is unique and satisfies \(f(y)\geq f(x_\star)+\frac{\mu}{2}d(x_\star,y)^2\) for all \(y\in C\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uniqueness and quadratic growth under the constant-speed minimizing-geodesic convention for strong convexity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Assume that for every constant-speed admissible minimizing geodesic \(\gamma:[0,1]\to C\), \[f(\gamma(t))\leq(1-t)f(\gamma(0))+tf(\gamma(1))-\frac{\mu}{2}t(1-t)d(\gamma(0),\gamma(1))^2.\] If \(x_\star\) minimizes \(f\), the first-order strong-convexity inequality at \(x_\star\) yields \[f(y)\geq f(x_\star)+\frac{\mu}{2}d(x_\star,y)^2\qquad(y\in C).\] Two distinct minimizers would make the right-hand side strictly greater than \(f(x_\star)\), a contradiction. Thus a minimizer, when it exists, is unique and enjoys quadratic growth.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Positive strong geodesic convexity makes any attained minimizer unique and forces objective growth at least quadratic in Riemannian distance from it.
knowledge_statements.title: Strong-Convexity Uniqueness Consequences

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The theorem fits the uniqueness-consequences topic, but the strong-convexity convention and quadratic-growth consequence need a specific authoritative citation. The contradiction argument is proof text.

children.title: Gradient Characterizations
children.top_down_role: Optimality characterizations expressed through Riemannian gradient information.

assumptions_latex: \(C\) lies in a normal neighborhood where each \(y\in C\) has a unique \(\operatorname{Log}_x(y)\) and the corresponding minimizing geodesic remains in \(C\).
\(f:C\to\mathbb R\) is differentiable.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f\) is geodesically convex on \(C\) if and only if \(f(y)\geq f(x)+\langle\operatorname{grad}f(x),\operatorname{Log}_x(y)\rangle_x\) for all \(x,y\in C\).

notation.meaning: inverse exponential vector from x to y

knowledge_statements.scope_note: First-order gradient inequality characterizing differentiable geodesic convexity on a uniquely geodesic normal domain.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Under the stated unique-geodesic convention, differentiable geodesic convexity is equivalent to the first-order support inequality \[f(y)\geq f(x)+\left\langle\operatorname{grad}f(x),\operatorname{Log}_x(y)\right\rangle_x\qquad\text{for all }x,y\in C.\] Here \(t\mapsto\operatorname{Exp}_x(t\operatorname{Log}_x(y))\) is the admissible minimizing geodesic from \(x\) to \(y\). In particular, at an interior point \(x_\star\), the equality \(\operatorname{grad}f(x_\star)=0\) makes the support inequality reduce to \(f(y)\geq f(x_\star)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: On a uniquely geodesic normal domain, differentiable geodesic convexity is equivalent to the Riemannian gradient supporting the objective along every logarithmic displacement.
knowledge_statements.title: Gradient Characterizations

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The condition kind fits the gradient-characterization leaf, but the equivalence depends on precise normal-domain and geodesic-selection hypotheses that have no cited support.

children.title: Variational-Inequality Characterizations
children.top_down_role: Optimality characterizations expressed through feasible geodesic comparisons.

assumptions_latex: \(C\subseteq\mathcal M\) is geodesically convex and contained in a normal neighborhood of each of its points.
\(f:C\to\mathbb R\) is differentiable and geodesically convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x_\star\in C\) minimizes \(f\) on \(C\) if and only if \(\langle\operatorname{grad}f(x_\star),\operatorname{Log}_{x_\star}(y)\rangle_{x_\star}\geq0\) for every \(y\in C\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Constrained first-order optimality expressed as a Riemannian variational inequality on a normal geodesically convex domain.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A point \(x_\star\in C\) is globally minimizing exactly when it solves the Riemannian variational inequality \[\left\langle\operatorname{grad}f(x_\star),\operatorname{Log}_{x_\star}(y)\right\rangle_{x_\star}\geq0\qquad\text{for every }y\in C.\] Necessity follows from the nonnegative right derivative of \(f\) along every feasible geodesic issuing from \(x_\star\). Sufficiency follows from the geodesic first-order support inequality. Unlike the unconstrained zero-gradient condition, this predicate also covers boundary minimizers whose gradients are nonzero but have no feasible descent direction.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A feasible point minimizes a differentiable geodesically convex objective exactly when its gradient has nonnegative inner product with every feasible logarithmic displacement.
knowledge_statements.title: Variational-Inequality Characterizations

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The variational-inequality condition fits the leaf and is plausible under the stated convexity assumptions, but necessity and sufficiency require an authoritative locator. The necessity/sufficiency explanation is proof text.

children.title: Characterization Equivalence Regimes
children.top_down_role: Domain plus convexity regimes supporting translation between the certificate families.

assumptions_latex: \(C\subseteq\mathcal M\) is an open, geodesically convex normal domain.
\(f:C\to\mathbb R\) is differentiable and geodesically convex.
\(x_\star\in C\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x_\star\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{C}f\iff\langle\operatorname{grad}f(x_\star),\operatorname{Log}_{x_\star}(y)\rangle_{x_\star}\geq0\ \forall y\in C\iff\operatorname{grad}f(x_\star)=0\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Equivalence of minimization, the variational inequality, and zero gradient for interior points of a normal convex domain.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For an open geodesically convex normal domain, the following statements are equivalent: \[x_\star\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in C}f(x),\qquad \left\langle\operatorname{grad}f(x_\star),\operatorname{Log}_{x_\star}(y)\right\rangle_{x_\star}\geq0\ \text{for all }y\in C,\qquad \operatorname{grad}f(x_\star)=0.\] Openness makes both sufficiently small positive and negative tangent perturbations feasible, so the variational inequality forces every component of the gradient to vanish. Geodesic convexity then makes zero gradient sufficient for global minimality. On a domain with boundary, only the first two characterizations remain equivalent in general.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For interior points of an open normal geodesically convex domain, global minimality, the Riemannian variational inequality, and zero gradient are equivalent.
knowledge_statements.title: Characterization Equivalence Regimes

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The theorem kind matches the equivalence-regime leaf, but the three-way equivalence and role of openness require cited support. The tangent-perturbation justification is proof text.

children.title: Characterization Gap Boundary
children.top_down_role: Geometric or domain conditions under which the certificate families diverge.

assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal M=\mathbb R\) with its Euclidean Riemannian metric.
\(C=[0,\infty)\) and \(f(x)=x\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(0\) is the unique constrained minimizer and satisfies the variational inequality, but \(\operatorname{grad}f(0)=1\neq0\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Concrete boundary example separating constrained variational-inequality optimality from the unconstrained zero-gradient characterization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The function \(f(x)=x\) is differentiable and geodesically convex on \(C=[0,\infty)\). Its unique minimizer is \(x_\star=0\), yet \(\operatorname{grad}f(0)=1\neq0\). For every \(y\in C\), however, \[\left\langle\operatorname{grad}f(0),\operatorname{Log}_0(y)\right\rangle=1\cdot y\geq0.\] Thus the variational inequality correctly characterizes the constrained minimizer while the zero-gradient characterization fails. The missing hypothesis is that the candidate be an interior point, or equivalently that both signs of every tangent direction be locally feasible.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At the boundary minimum of f(x)=x on the nonnegative half-line, the gradient is nonzero while the constrained variational inequality still holds.
knowledge_statements.title: Characterization Gap Boundary

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The counterexample kind exactly fits the characterization-gap leaf and the Euclidean example is internally consistent, but the record supplies no admissible evidence. Its verification narrative is proof text.

children.title: Domain Admissibility Boundary
children.top_down_role: Failures caused by nonconvex, incomplete, disconnected, or locally restricted domains.

assumptions_latex: \((\mathcal M,g)\) is a Riemannian manifold.
\(C\subseteq\mathcal M\) is the domain on which logarithmic first-order formulas are to be used.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The formulas are unambiguous on \(C\) when \(C\) is strongly geodesically convex and \(C\cap\operatorname{Cut}(x)=\varnothing\) for every \(x\in C\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sufficient domain conditions for single-valued logarithms and feasible minimizing geodesics.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A sufficient admissibility condition is that for every \(x,y\in C\) there exists a unique minimizing geodesic \(\gamma_{xy}:[0,1]\to\mathcal M\), its image lies in \(C\), and \(y\notin\operatorname{Cut}(x)\). Then \(\operatorname{Log}_x(y)=\dot\gamma_{xy}(0)\) is single-valued and varies smoothly locally, while \(\gamma_{xy}(t)=\operatorname{Exp}_x(t\operatorname{Log}_x(y))\) remains feasible. These properties make gradient support inequalities and variational inequalities intrinsically well-defined for every ordered pair in \(C\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A strongly geodesically convex domain avoiding pairwise cut loci provides unique feasible minimizing geodesics and single-valued logarithms for first-order optimality formulas.
knowledge_statements.title: Domain Admissibility Boundary

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The condition kind fits the admissibility-boundary leaf, but strong geodesic convexity, cut-locus avoidance, uniqueness, and local smoothness of the logarithm require a precise source and consistent terminology.

children.title: Geodesic-Selection Boundary
children.top_down_role: Failures caused by nonunique, unavailable, or representation-sensitive geodesic choices.

assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal M=S^1\) has its standard metric.
\(x=1\), \(y=-1\), and \(f(e^{i\theta})=\sin\theta\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The two minimizing logarithms give opposite first-order pairings, so a logarithmic inequality is selection-dependent at \((x,y)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Antipodal circle example showing that first-order inequalities depend on geodesic selection when logarithms are multivalued.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: At the antipodal pair \(x=1\) and \(y=-1\), there are two minimizing geodesics and hence two logarithmic vectors, identified in \(T_xS^1\cong\mathbb R\) as \(\operatorname{Log}_x(y)\in\{\pi,-\pi\}\). Since \(\operatorname{grad}f(x)=1\), the corresponding pairings are \[\left\langle\operatorname{grad}f(x),\pi\right\rangle=\pi,\qquad \left\langle\operatorname{grad}f(x),-\pi\right\rangle=-\pi.\] Therefore an inequality stated using an unspecified minimizing logarithm has no definite truth value. A theory must require uniqueness or explicitly quantify over, or select among, admissible geodesics.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At antipodal circle points, two minimizing logarithms have opposite signs, so the same gradient inequality can hold or fail depending on the chosen geodesic.
knowledge_statements.title: Geodesic-Selection Boundary

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure-boundary kind and antipodal-circle example fit the leaf, but no source documents the multivalued logarithm and selection-dependence claim. The explicit calculation is proof text.

children.title: Cut-Locus Interference
children.top_down_role: Selection ambiguity plus loss of smooth comparison near cut-locus regimes.

assumptions_latex: \(S^n\) has the standard round metric, with north pole \(N\) and south pole \(S\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(h\) is not differentiable at \(S\), and \(\operatorname{Log}_S(N)\) is multivalued; gradient-log characterizations cannot be applied there.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Round-sphere example where the cut locus destroys smooth squared-distance and single-valued logarithmic formulas.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: On the round sphere, \(\operatorname{Cut}(N)=\{S\}\), and infinitely many minimizing meridians join \(N\) to \(S\). On \(S^n\setminus\{S\}\), the squared-distance function is smooth and satisfies \[\operatorname{grad}h(x)=-\operatorname{Log}_x(N).\] At \(S\), the inverse exponential vector toward \(N\) is not unique and \(h\) is not differentiable. Consequently, first-order support or variational-inequality characterizations involving \(\operatorname{grad}h(S)\) or a single \(\operatorname{Log}_S(N)\) are undefined. Excluding the cut locus, or adopting a nonsmooth set-valued formulation, is necessary.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At the sphere's antipode, squared distance is nonsmooth and the minimizing logarithm is multivalued, invalidating ordinary gradient-log optimality formulas.
knowledge_statements.title: Cut-Locus Interference

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure-boundary kind fits cut-locus interference, and the sphere example is plausible, but the smoothness domain, gradient identity, and nondifferentiability at the antipode need an authoritative locator. The explanatory derivation is proof text.

children.title: Domain–Geodesic Compatibility
children.top_down_role: Conditions governing whether selected geodesics remain inside the admissible region.

knowledge_statements.title: Domain–Geodesic Compatibility
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Compatibility needed to formulate geodesic convexity on a constrained domain.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \((M,g)\) be a complete Riemannian manifold and let \(D\subseteq M\). The domain \(D\) is geodesically compatible if, for every \(x,y\in D\), there exists a minimizing geodesic \(\gamma_{xy}:[0,1]\to M\) satisfying \(\gamma_{xy}(0)=x\), \(\gamma_{xy}(1)=y\), and \(\gamma_{xy}([0,1])\subseteq D\). If a prescribed family \(\Gamma\) of geodesics is used, compatibility additionally requires that such a curve can be chosen from \(\Gamma(x,y)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every two domain points must admit an admissible minimizing geodesic that remains entirely inside the domain.
assumptions_latex: \((M,g)\) is a complete Riemannian manifold.
\(D\subseteq M\) is nonempty.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\forall x,y\in D\;\exists\gamma_{xy}:\gamma_{xy}([0,1])\subseteq D\) with \(\gamma_{xy}\) minimizing from \(x\) to \(y\).

notation.meaning: A minimizing geodesic from x to y
Prescribed admissible geodesics joining x and y

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard definition of a geodesically convex domain

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The condition fits the terminal container and is mathematically coherent, but no inspectable source establishes the intended meaning of “geodesically compatible,” especially the optional prescribed-family variant.

knowledge_statements.title: Global Logarithmic Geometry
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Cartan–Hadamard form giving a globally defined logarithm map.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \((M,g)\) be a connected, complete, simply connected finite-dimensional Riemannian manifold with sectional curvature \(K\leq 0\). For every \(x\in M\), the exponential map \(\operatorname{Exp}_x:T_xM\to M\) is a global diffeomorphism. Consequently, \(\operatorname{Log}_x=\operatorname{Exp}_x^{-1}\) is defined and smooth on all of \(M\), every \(y\in M\) is joined to \(x\) by the unique minimizing geodesic \(t\mapsto\operatorname{Exp}_x(t\operatorname{Log}_x y)\), and \(d(x,y)=\|\operatorname{Log}_x y\|_x\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: On a Hadamard manifold, every exponential map is globally invertible, yielding unique minimizing geodesics and globally defined logarithms.
assumptions_latex: \((M,g)\) is connected, complete, simply connected, and finite-dimensional.
The sectional curvature satisfies \(K\leq 0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{Exp}_x:T_xM\to M\) is a diffeomorphism for every \(x\in M\), with \(d(x,y)=\|\operatorname{Log}_x y\|_x\).

notation.meaning: Global inverse of the exponential map at x

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The Cartan–Hadamard statement and theorem content are appropriate, but the record supplies no authoritative theorem citation or locator.

knowledge_statements.title: Nonpositive-Curvature Convexity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Convexity of squared distance on a Hadamard manifold.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \((M,g)\) be a Hadamard manifold. For every \(z\in M\), the function \(x\mapsto \tfrac12 d(x,z)^2\) is geodesically \(1\)-strongly convex: for the unique geodesic \(\gamma:[0,1]\to M\) from \(x\) to \(y\), \[\frac12d(\gamma(t),z)^2\leq(1-t)\frac12d(x,z)^2+t\frac12d(y,z)^2-\frac12t(1-t)d(x,y)^2,\qquad 0\leq t\leq1.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Nonpositive curvature makes half the squared distance globally strongly geodesically convex.
assumptions_latex: \((M,g)\) is complete, simply connected, with sectional curvature \(K\leq0\).
\(x,y,z\in M\) and \(t\in[0,1]\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x\mapsto \tfrac12d(x,z)^2\) is geodesically \(1\)-strongly convex.

notation.meaning: Unique geodesic from x to y

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: CAT(0) squared-distance inequality for Hadamard manifolds

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The squared-distance convexity inequality is appropriate for a finite-dimensional Hadamard manifold, but its normalization and hypotheses require an authoritative CAT(0) or Hessian-comparison locator.

knowledge_statements.title: Hadamard First-Order Rate Families
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Deterministic Riemannian gradient-descent rates for smooth geodesically convex objectives.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f:M\to\mathbb R\) be geodesically convex on a Hadamard manifold, attain its minimum at \(x_*\), and have \(L\)-Lipschitz Riemannian gradient. For \(x_{k+1}=\operatorname{Exp}_{x_k}(-L^{-1}\operatorname{grad}f(x_k))\), assume the iterates remain in a region where the standard descent and geodesic comparison inequalities used by the analysis hold. Then the family has sublinear objective complexity \(f(x_k)-f(x_*)=O(Ld(x_0,x_*)^2/k)\). Under \(\mu\)-strong geodesic convexity, the corresponding rate is geometric, \(f(x_k)-f(x_*)=O((1-\mu/L)^k)\), with curvature-dependent constants where comparison bounds are required.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Riemannian gradient descent has sublinear convex and geometric strongly convex rates, with constants potentially affected by curvature.
assumptions_latex: \(M\) is Hadamard and \(f\) has \(L\)-Lipschitz Riemannian gradient.
\(f\) is geodesically convex and attains a minimum.
Required comparison inequalities hold along the iterates.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f(x_k)-f(x_*)=O(k^{-1})\), or \(O((1-\mu/L)^k)\) under \(\mu\)-strong geodesic convexity.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The complexity-bound kind fits, but “standard descent and geodesic comparison inequalities” is not an explicit hypothesis, and the claimed rates depend on the precise smoothness, curvature, bounded-region, and indexing conventions. A specific rate theorem is required.

knowledge_statements.title: Curvature-Dependent Oracle Limitations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Why Euclidean-style uniform oracle bounds need geometric control.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix \(z\) in a Hadamard manifold and set \(h_z(x)=\tfrac12d(x,z)^2\). Although \(\operatorname{grad}h_z(x)=-\operatorname{Log}_x z\), a sectional-curvature lower bound \(K\geq-\kappa\) yields comparison factors of order \(\sqrt{\kappa}\,r\coth(\sqrt{\kappa}\,r)\) for the transverse Hessian at distance \(r=d(x,z)\). This factor is unbounded as \(r\to\infty\) when \(\kappa>0\). Hence first-order oracle guarantees requiring a radius-independent Euclidean smoothness constant cannot generally hold on unbounded negatively curved domains without diameter, curvature, or local-region restrictions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Negative curvature can make squared-distance smoothness constants grow with radius, preventing radius-independent Euclidean oracle guarantees.
assumptions_latex: \(M\) is Hadamard with sectional curvature bounded below by \(-\kappa\), where \(\kappa>0\).
The optimization domain permits \(d(x,z)\to\infty\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: No radius-independent Hessian or gradient-Lipschitz bound for \(h_z\) follows solely from the curvature bound.

notation.meaning: Magnitude of the negative curvature lower bound

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure-boundary kind fits, but the exact Hessian-comparison factor and the inference to oracle limitations depend on curvature-bound direction and convention. These claims need inspectable Hessian-comparison and oracle references.

knowledge_statements.title: Strict-Saddle Landscapes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uniform strict-saddle condition for a smooth manifold objective.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f:M\to\mathbb R\) be twice continuously differentiable. For constants \(\alpha,\beta,\gamma>0\), \(f\) has an \((\alpha,\beta,\gamma)\)-strict-saddle landscape if every \(x\in M\) satisfies at least one of: \(\|\operatorname{grad}f(x)\|_x\geq\alpha\); \(\lambda_{\min}(\operatorname{Hess}f(x))\leq-\beta\); or \(d(x,\mathcal X_*)\leq\gamma\), where \(\mathcal X_*\) is a specified set of local minimizers whose neighborhoods contain no nonminimal critical points. In particular, every critical point outside those neighborhoods has a direction of strictly negative Riemannian curvature.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every point has a large gradient, a negative-curvature direction, or lies near an isolated local-minimum region.
assumptions_latex: \(M\) is a finite-dimensional Riemannian manifold.
\(\mathcal X_*\) is a specified set of local minimizers.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every critical point outside the \(\gamma\)-neighborhood of \(\mathcal X_*\) satisfies \(\lambda_{\min}(\operatorname{Hess}f)\leq-\beta\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: common quantitative strict-saddle condition adapted to a Riemannian manifold

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The condition kind fits, but quantitative strict-saddle definitions vary, and the stated “neighborhoods” are not formally identified with the metric gamma-neighborhood used in the conclusion. A manifold-specific source is needed to fix the intended convention.

knowledge_statements.title: Symmetry-Induced Critical Manifolds
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Critical orbits generated by invariance under a Lie-group action.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let a Lie group \(G\) act smoothly and isometrically on \((M,g)\), and let \(f:M\to\mathbb R\) satisfy \(f(g\cdot x)=f(x)\) for all \(g\in G\). If \(x\) is critical, then every point of the orbit \(G\cdot x\) is critical. Moreover, for every orbit-tangent vector \(v\in T_x(G\cdot x)\), \(df_x[v]=0\); at a critical point, \(\operatorname{Hess}f(x)[v]=0\). Thus positive-dimensional symmetry orbits form critical submanifolds with Hessian zero modes along their tangent spaces.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An invariant objective carries each critical point into a critical orbit, with Hessian zero directions tangent to that orbit.
assumptions_latex: \(G\) acts smoothly and isometrically on \((M,g)\).
\(f\in C^2(M)\) is \(G\)-invariant.
\(x\) is a critical point and \(G\cdot x\) is an embedded orbit.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(G\cdot x\subseteq\operatorname{Crit}(f)\) and \(T_x(G\cdot x)\subseteq\ker(\operatorname{Hess}f(x))\).

notation.meaning: Orbit of x under the group action

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The property is mathematically plausible and fits the container, but the critical-orbit and Hessian-kernel conclusions lack an inspectable equivariant critical-point or Lie-group-action source.

children.title: Degenerate Critical Regions
children.top_down_role: Critical regions with rank-deficient or inconclusive local curvature structure.

knowledge_statements.title: Degenerate Critical Regions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Critical sets where second-order nondegeneracy fails.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f\in C^2(M)\). A subset \(C\subseteq M\) is a degenerate critical region of \(f\) if \(C\subseteq\operatorname{Crit}(f)=\{x:\operatorname{grad}f(x)=0\}\) and every \(x\in C\) has a nontrivial Hessian kernel, \(\ker(\operatorname{Hess}f(x))\neq\{0\}\). If \(C\) is an embedded critical submanifold, degeneracy beyond its unavoidable tangent directions occurs when \(\ker(\operatorname{Hess}f(x))\supsetneq T_xC\) for some \(x\in C\); equality at every point is the Morse–Bott nondegeneracy condition.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A degenerate critical region consists of stationary points with Hessian zero modes, possibly exceeding tangent directions of the critical set.
assumptions_latex: \(M\) is a finite-dimensional Riemannian manifold.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(C\subseteq\operatorname{Crit}(f)\) and \(\ker(\operatorname{Hess}f(x))\neq\{0\}\) for all \(x\in C\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: Hessian-kernel definition of critical-point degeneracy

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition kind fits, but “degenerate critical region” is not standardized, and the record uses both pointwise Hessian degeneracy and degeneracy beyond tangent directions. A source must establish the intended taxonomic distinction from Morse–Bott critical manifolds.

children.title: Flat Critical Regions
children.top_down_role: Critical regions exhibiting weak variation across extended manifold directions.

knowledge_statements.title: Flat Critical Regions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Critical regions on which the objective has locally vanishing variation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f\in C^2(M)\) and let \(C\subseteq M\) be a connected embedded submanifold. The set \(C\) is a flat critical region if \(\operatorname{grad}f(x)=0\) for every \(x\in C\) and \(f|_C\) is constant. Its intrinsic first and second derivatives therefore vanish along \(C\); equivalently, for each \(x\in C\) and \(v\in T_xC\), \(df_x[v]=0\) and \(\operatorname{Hess}f(x)[v]=0\). Normal Hessian eigenvalues may be nonzero, so flatness along \(C\) does not imply ambient local constancy.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A flat critical region is a connected stationary submanifold with constant objective value and zero Hessian action along tangent directions.
assumptions_latex: \(M\) is a Riemannian manifold and \(f\in C^2(M)\).
\(C\subseteq M\) is a connected embedded submanifold.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f|_C\) is constant and \(T_xC\subseteq\ker(\operatorname{Hess}f(x))\) for every \(x\in C\).

notation.meaning: Tangent space of C at x

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition is internally coherent, but stationarity on a connected submanifold already entails constancy and tangent Hessian zero modes. A source is required to show that this is the intended, nonredundant meaning of “flat critical region.”

children.title: Higher-Order Critical Structure
children.top_down_role: Landscape distinctions visible only beyond ordinary first- or second-order diagnostics.

knowledge_statements.title: Higher-Order Critical Structure
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Leading covariant Taylor term at a Hessian-degenerate critical point.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(f\in C^p(M)\), let \(x\) satisfy \(\operatorname{grad}f(x)=0\), and suppose \(
abla^j f(x)=0\) for \(2\leq j<p\) while \(
abla^p f(x)
eq0\), with \(p\geq3\). In normal coordinates, for sufficiently small \(v\in T_xM\), \[f(\operatorname{Exp}_x v)=f(x)+ rac{1}{p!}
abla^p f(x)[v,\ldots,v]+o(\|v\|_x^p).\] The homogeneous form \(v\mapsto
abla^p f(x)[v^p]\) is the leading local critical structure and determines the first nonvanishing directional variation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: When gradient and lower derivatives vanish, the first nonzero covariant derivative gives the leading local shape of the objective.
assumptions_latex: \(f\in C^p(M)\) for an integer \(p\geq3\).
\(\nabla^j f(x)=0\) for \(1\leq j<p\).
\(\nabla^p f(x)\neq0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f(\operatorname{Exp}_xv)-f(x)=\frac1{p!}\nabla^pf(x)[v^p]+o(\|v\|_x^p)\).

notation.meaning: j-th covariant derivative of f at x
p repeated arguments equal to v

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: covariant Taylor expansion in normal coordinates

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The representation kind fits and the displayed leading-order expansion is plausible under the stated vanishing assumptions, but a precise Riemannian Taylor theorem and covariant-derivative convention must be cited.

children.title: Critical-Region Persistence
children.top_down_role: Stability of extended critical behavior under perturbation or symmetry reduction.

knowledge_statements.title: Critical-Region Persistence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Structural instability of degenerate critical regions under perturbation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Degenerate critical regions need not persist under arbitrarily small smooth perturbations. For example, on \(M=\mathbb R^2\), \(f_0(x,y)=x^2\) has the flat critical line \(C=\{(0,y):y\in\mathbb R\}\). For every \(\varepsilon>0\), the perturbation \(f_\varepsilon(x,y)=x^2+\varepsilon y^2\) is arbitrarily close to \(f_0\) on compact sets in the \(C^2\) topology as \(\varepsilon\downarrow0\), but \(\operatorname{Crit}(f_\varepsilon)=\{(0,0)\}\). Persistence therefore requires additional structure, such as preserved symmetry or an appropriate nondegeneracy condition.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A flat critical line can collapse to one critical point under an arbitrarily small smooth perturbation, so degeneracy alone gives no persistence.
assumptions_latex: \(M=\mathbb R^2\) with its Euclidean metric.
\(f_\varepsilon(x,y)=x^2+\varepsilon y^2\) for \(\varepsilon\geq0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{Crit}(f_0)=\{0\}\times\mathbb R\), whereas \(\operatorname{Crit}(f_\varepsilon)=\{(0,0)\}\) for every \(\varepsilon>0\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The counterexample is directly checkable and the failure-boundary kind fits. However, the broader assertion about which additional structures yield persistence is not supported by an inspectable source.

knowledge_statements.title: Kurdyka–Łojasiewicz Interface
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Riemannian KL inequality near a critical level.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f:M\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper and lower semicontinuous, and let \(\bar x\in\operatorname{dom}\partial f\). The function has the Kurdyka–Łojasiewicz property at \(\bar x\) if there exist a neighborhood \(U\) of \(\bar x\), \(\eta>0\), and a concave function \(\varphi:[0,\eta)\to\mathbb R_+\), continuous at \(0\), with \(\varphi(0)=0\), \(\varphi\in C^1((0,\eta))\), and \(\varphi'>0\), such that \[\varphi'(f(x)-f(\bar x))\,\operatorname{dist}(0,\partial f(x))\geq1\] whenever \(x\in U\) and \(f(\bar x)<f(x)<f(\bar x)+\eta\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Near a critical level, objective-value decrease controls the distance from zero to the Riemannian subdifferential.
assumptions_latex: \(M\) is a finite-dimensional Riemannian manifold.
\(f\) is proper and lower semicontinuous.
\(\bar x\in\operatorname{dom}\partial f\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\varphi'(f(x)-f(\bar x))\operatorname{dist}(0,\partial f(x))\geq1\) locally above \(f(\bar x)\).

notation.meaning: Minimum tangent-space norm of a subgradient

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The condition kind fits, but the limiting Riemannian subdifferential is only described as “chosen.” The KL formulation depends on that convention and requires a manifold-specific definition with a precise locator.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Retraction-based deterministic Riemannian gradient descent with a constant step size.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given \(x_0\in\mathcal M\), a fixed step \(\alpha>0\), a tolerance \(\varepsilon\geq0\), and an iteration limit \(K\), compute \(g_k=\operatorname{grad}f(x_k)\). If \(\lVert g_k\rVert_{x_k}\leq\varepsilon\) or \(k=K\), return \(x_k\). Otherwise set \(\eta_k=-\alpha g_k\in T_{x_k}\mathcal M\) and update \[x_{k+1}=R_{x_k}(\eta_k).\] The method uses the same scalar step at every accepted iteration; feasibility on \(\mathcal M\) is supplied by the retraction rather than by an ambient-space projection.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Starting from a manifold point, repeatedly retract a fixed multiple of the negative Riemannian gradient, stopping at the requested stationarity tolerance or iteration limit.

children.title: Armijo Acceptance Criteria
children.top_down_role: Sufficient-decrease interfaces for retraction-based trial points.

assumptions_latex: \(f:\mathcal M\to\mathbb R\) is differentiable, \(x\in\mathcal M\), and \(R_x\) is defined along the trial step.
\(\eta\in T_x\mathcal M\) is a descent direction: \(\langle\operatorname{grad}f(x),\eta\rangle_x<0\).
The sufficient-decrease parameter satisfies \(c\in(0,1)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A trial step \(t>0\) is accepted exactly when \(f(R_x(t\eta))\leq f(x)+ct\langle\operatorname{grad}f(x),\eta\rangle_x\).

notation.meaning: Current manifold point and tangent search direction

knowledge_statements.scope_note: One-sided Armijo sufficient decrease along a retraction curve.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a trial length \(t>0\), define the retraction curve \(\gamma(t)=R_x(t\eta)\). The Armijo acceptance predicate is \[f(\gamma(t))\leq f(x)+ct\langle\operatorname{grad}f(x),\eta\rangle_x.\] Since \(\eta\) is a descent direction, the right-hand correction is negative. Thus acceptance requires an objective decrease at least equal to the fraction \(c\) of the decrease predicted by the first-order directional model at \(t=0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Accept a trial step when its actual objective value achieves at least the prescribed fraction of the first-order decrease along the retraction curve.
knowledge_statements.title: Armijo Acceptance Criteria

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The condition role and Armijo predicate are mathematically standard and fit the leaf, but no inspectable Riemannian optimization source is cited.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: General Euclidean sufficient-decrease backtracking along a search direction.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix \(\beta,\sigma\in(0,1)\). Let \(m_k\) be the smallest integer \(m\ge 0\) such that \[f(x^k)-f(x^k+\beta^m d^k)\ge -\sigma\beta^m\nabla f(x^k)^\top d^k.\] Set \(\alpha^k=\beta^{m_k}\); equivalently, test \(1,\beta,\beta^2,\ldots\) until the sufficient-decrease inequality holds.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Fix contraction and sufficient-decrease parameters between zero and one. Test geometrically decreasing steps 1, beta, beta squared, and so on, and accept the first step satisfying the Armijo inequality.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given \(x\), a descent direction \(\eta\), parameters \(c,\rho\in(0,1)\), initial trial \(t_0>0\), and evaluation limit \(J\), inspect \(t_j=t_0\rho^j\) for \(j=0,\ldots,J\).
