knowledge_statements.title: Distributed Manifold Optimization Interface
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Abstract synchronous interface for consensus-based optimization over a common Riemannian manifold.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,E)\) be a connected communication graph, let \((\mathcal M,g)\) be a Riemannian manifold, and let agent \(i\in V\) hold a differentiable function \(f_i:\mathcal M\to\mathbb R\). A distributed manifold optimization interface for minimizing \(F(x)=\sum_{i\in V}f_i(x)\) consists of local states \(x_i\in\mathcal M\), neighbor-message maps, tangent-space comparison maps \(\mathcal T_{x_j\to x_i}:T_{x_j}\mathcal M\to T_{x_i}\mathcal M\), and feasible update maps \(R_{x_i}:T_{x_i}\mathcal M\to\mathcal M\). Communication is restricted to edges of \(G\), and a consensual output satisfies \(x_i=x_j=x_\star\) for every \((i,j)\in E\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Agents optimize local objectives on one manifold, communicate only with graph neighbors, compare tangent data through transports, update by retractions, and seek a common manifold point.

\((\mathcal M,g)\) is a Riemannian manifold.

knowledge_statements.title: Communication-Avoiding Geometry Interface
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Interface separating local geometric computation from infrequent synchronization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a distributed problem on a Riemannian manifold \(\mathcal M\), a communication-avoiding geometry interface with synchronization period \(s\geq1\) permits each worker to perform \(s\) local oracle, tangent-space, and retraction operations before exchanging data. At synchronization, every transmitted tangent vector must be tagged by its base point and converted to a common tangent space by a specified transport, while manifold points must be combined by a specified intrinsic aggregation map \(A:\mathcal M^m\to\mathcal M\). The interface is geometrically consistent when all synchronized quantities are compared in one tangent space and every returned iterate lies in \(\mathcal M\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Workers perform several local geometric updates per communication round; synchronization explicitly transports tangent data to a common base point and aggregates manifold-valued states feasibly.

\(s\in\mathbb N\) is the number of local steps between synchronizations.

knowledge_statements.title: Singular Constraint Sets
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Breakdown of the regular-level-set manifold model for equality constraints.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F:N\to\mathbb R^m\) be smooth on a smooth manifold \(N\), and set \(C=F^{-1}(0)\). A point \(x\in C\) is singular for this constraint representation when \(\operatorname{rank}DF_x<m\). If the rank of \(DF\) is not locally constant on \(C\) near \(x\), the regular-level-set theorem supplies neither a single local dimension nor the tangent identity \(T_yC=\ker DF_y\) throughout a neighborhood of \(x\). Consequently, algorithms requiring one smooth embedded constraint manifold and a fixed-dimensional tangent bundle cross their modeling boundary at such points.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A constraint point is singular when its Jacobian loses rank; varying nearby rank destroys the standard fixed-dimensional level-set manifold model used by smooth manifold algorithms.
assumptions_latex: \(F:N\to\mathbb R^m\) is smooth.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Nonconstant constraint rank near \(x\) invalidates the regular-level-set manifold model locally.

notation.meaning: Differential of the constraint map at x.

review_flags: An authoritative differential-topology locator for regular and singular level sets is required.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure-boundary role is appropriate, and the regular-level-set limitation is stated cautiously. No differential-topology source or inspectable locator is supplied for the regular-value, constant-rank, and tangent-space claims.

children.title: Smooth Boundary Strata
children.top_down_role: Smooth codimension-one boundary regions affecting feasible manifold motion.

knowledge_statements.title: Smooth Boundary Strata
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Depth-one stratum of a smooth manifold with corners.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(M\) be an \(n\)-dimensional smooth manifold with corners. A point \(x\in M\) lies in a smooth boundary stratum when it has depth one: in an adapted chart \(\phi:U\to[0,\infty)\times\mathbb R^{n-1}\), one has \(\phi(x)=(0,z)\), and exactly one boundary coordinate vanishes locally. The associated stratum is locally \(S=\phi^{-1}(\{0\}\times\mathbb R^{n-1})\), an embedded \((n-1)\)-manifold without boundary. Its feasible tangent cone is a half-space whose lineality space is \(T_xS\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A smooth boundary stratum consists locally of points where exactly one boundary coordinate is active; it is a codimension-one embedded manifold with a half-space feasible tangent cone.
assumptions_latex: \(M\) is an \(n\)-dimensional smooth manifold with corners.
\(x\in M\) has depth one.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The local boundary stratum through \(x\) is an embedded manifold of dimension \(n-1\).

notation.meaning: Tangent space of the boundary stratum.

review_flags: A source on manifolds with corners and depth strata is required.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition matches the smooth-boundary-stratum leaf and is mathematically plausible under the standard manifold-with-corners convention. A cited source is required for depth strata and for the convention-dependent feasible tangent-cone statement.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Positive-depth strata where multiple boundary coordinates are simultaneously active.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(M\) be an \(n\)-dimensional smooth manifold with corners. A point \(x\in M\) has corner depth \(k\) when, in an adapted local chart with coordinates in \([0,\infty)^k\times\mathbb R^{n-k}\), the first \(k\) coordinates vanish at \(x\). The connected components of the depth-\(k\) set form corner strata. Locally, the stratum through \(x\) is an embedded manifold of dimension \(n-k\), while its feasible tangent cone is linearly equivalent to \([0,\infty)^k\times\mathbb R^{n-k}\) and is not a vector space when \(k>0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A depth-k corner has k active boundary coordinates; its stratum has codimension k, and its feasible directions form a cone rather than a tangent vector space.

children.title: Active-Stratum Transitions
children.top_down_role: Transitions among interior, boundary, and corner strata during optimization.

knowledge_statements.title: Active-Stratum Transitions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Iterate transitions between strata having different active boundary sets.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(M\) be a manifold with corners stratified by active boundary sets, and let \((x_k)\subset M\) be an optimization trajectory. An active-stratum transition occurs at index \(k\) when \(x_k\in S_I\), \(x_{k+1}\in S_J\), and \(I\neq J\), where \(S_I\) denotes the stratum with active set \(I\). If \(|I|\neq|J|\), then \(T_{x_k}S_I\) and \(T_{x_{k+1}}S_J\) have different dimensions. Thus a search model confined to one stratum cannot be transferred across the transition without an explicit rule for changing tangent spaces and feasible cones.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A transition occurs when consecutive iterates have different active boundary sets; changing stratum dimension invalidates an unchanged fixed-stratum tangent model.
assumptions_latex: \(M\) is stratified by active boundary sets.
\(x_k\in S_I\) and \(x_{k+1}\in S_J\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: When \(I\neq J\), a fixed-stratum search model requires an explicit transition rule.

children.title: Boundary-Compatible Search Geometry
children.top_down_role: Search geometries compatible with local boundary or corner structure.

knowledge_statements.title: Boundary-Compatible Search Geometry
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Feasibility and first-order descent conditions for searches at boundary points.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\) be a closed feasible subset of a Riemannian manifold \(N\), let \(x\in C\), and let \(T_C(x)\subset T_xN\) be its contingent tangent cone. A search geometry is boundary-compatible at \(x\) if its admissible direction set \(D_x\) satisfies \(D_x\subseteq T_C(x)\), its update map \(R_x:D_x\supset U_x\to C\) obeys \(R_x(0)=x\) and \(DR_x(0)[v]=v\) for \(v\in D_x\), and a chosen search direction \(v\) satisfies \(df_x[v]<0\) unless a first-order stationarity test holds. These conditions enforce local feasibility and first-order consistency.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Boundary-compatible search uses only contingent feasible directions, maps them back into the feasible set with first-order consistency, and selects descent unless stationarity is detected.
assumptions_latex: \(C\) is closed in a Riemannian manifold \(N\).
\(f:N\to\mathbb R\) is differentiable near \(x\in C\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The search step is locally feasible and agrees to first order with its admissible tangent direction.

notation.meaning: Contingent tangent cone of C at x.

review_flags: No supplied source supports this manifold-boundary search condition.
Differentiability of the cone-domain update may require a convention-specific formulation.

The first-order stationarity test is also unspecified. A source and convention-specific formulation are needed before the mathematical condition can be fixed reliably.

knowledge_statements.title: Stratified-Space Interfaces
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Computational interface for optimization across a locally finite smooth stratification.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X=\bigsqcup_{\alpha\in A}S_\alpha\) be a locally finite stratification whose strata are smooth manifolds. A stratified-space optimization interface assigns to each \(x\in S_\alpha\) a stratum tangent space \(T_xS_\alpha\), a stratumwise derivative of the objective, a feasible update map into \(X\), and transition maps for comparing models when an update enters \(S_\beta\neq S_\alpha\). The interface must expose the incident-stratum relation \(S_\beta\cap\overline{S_\alpha}\neq\varnothing\) and must not identify tangent spaces of unequal-dimensional strata without an explicit embedding, projection, or limiting-cone rule.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A stratified optimization interface supplies smooth calculus within each stratum and explicit feasible transition rules between incident strata, without silently equating incompatible tangent spaces.
assumptions_latex: \(X=\bigsqcup_{\alpha\in A}S_\alpha\) is a locally finite smooth stratification.
The objective is differentiable on every stratum.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Optimization models are defined stratumwise and transferred between incident strata only through specified transition maps.

notation.meaning: Tangent space within the active stratum.

review_flags: An authoritative source for stratified optimization interfaces and transition calculus is required.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: A definition is appropriate for this interface leaf, but the required incident-stratum exposure and transition maps form an uncited constructed computational contract. A source on optimization over stratified spaces is needed to determine the correct hypotheses and interface elements.

knowledge_statements.title: Rank-Changing Trajectories
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Loss of a fixed-rank manifold model along matrix-valued trajectories.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X:[0,1]\to\mathbb R^{m\times n}\) be continuous and suppose \(\operatorname{rank}X(t)=r\) for \(t<t_\star\) but \(\operatorname{rank}X(t_\star)=q\neq r\). The fixed-rank set \(\mathcal M_r=\{Y:\operatorname{rank}Y=r\}\) is a smooth manifold of dimension \(r(m+n-r)\), but \(X(t_\star)\notin\mathcal M_r\). Hence a retraction, tangent projection, or Hessian model defined only on \(\mathcal M_r\) is not defined at the rank-changing point. Continuing the trajectory requires a rank-adaptive, stratified, or closure-based model.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: When a matrix trajectory changes rank, it leaves its fixed-rank manifold, so fixed-rank tangent projections, retractions, and Hessian models cease to apply at the transition.
assumptions_latex: \(X:[0,1]\to\mathbb R^{m\times n}\) is continuous.
The rank changes from \(r\) to \(q\neq r\) at \(t_\star\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The fixed-rank manifold model \(\mathcal M_r\) breaks down at \(X(t_\star)\).

notation.meaning: Manifold of matrices having rank exactly r.

review_flags: A source for fixed-rank manifold dimension and rank-stratified closure behavior is required.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure-boundary kind and fixed-rank dimension formula fit the node. The record has no source for the smooth fixed-rank manifold, its dimension, or the breakdown of manifold-specific operators at a rank transition.

children.title: Geodesic Nonuniqueness
children.top_down_role: Regimes admitting multiple relevant geodesic connections between manifold points.

knowledge_statements.title: Geodesic Nonuniqueness
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure of unique minimizing-geodesic selection between two manifold points.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \((M,g)\) be a complete connected Riemannian manifold and let \(p,q\in M\). Geodesic nonuniqueness occurs when there exist distinct tangent vectors \(v,w\in T_pM\) with \(\exp_p(v)=\exp_p(w)=q\) and \(\|v\|_p=\|w\|_p=d(p,q)\). Then the minimizing logarithm \(\log_p(q)\) is set-valued, so any optimization construction requiring a uniquely selected minimizing displacement from \(p\) to \(q\)—for example, an intrinsic interpolation or a gradient formula based on \(-\log_p(q)\)—is not intrinsically single-valued without an additional selection rule.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Two distinct shortest geodesics from p to q make the minimizing logarithm set-valued, so algorithms using a unique intrinsic displacement need a selection rule.
assumptions_latex: \((M,g)\) is complete and connected.
\(p,q\in M\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Distinct minimizing initial velocities make \(\log_p(q)\) nonunique.

notation.meaning: Riemannian distance between p and q.
Set of minimizing initial velocities from p to q.

review_flags: A Riemannian-geometry source for minimizing geodesics and the multivalued logarithm is required.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure-boundary role is correct, and the explicit existence of distinct minimizing initial velocities precisely captures the claimed nonuniqueness. An authoritative Riemannian-geometry source with a specific locator is still required.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Validity boundary encountered when an iterate, trial point, or data point lies in the cut locus of a base point.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \((M,g)\) be a complete connected Riemannian manifold and fix \(p\in M\). The cut locus \(\operatorname{Cut}(p)\) consists of endpoints at which minimizing geodesics issuing from \(p\) reach their maximal interval of minimality. A cut-locus encounter occurs when an iterate, trial point, or data point \(q\), used relative to \(p\), satisfies \(q\in\operatorname{Cut}(p)\). At such a point, no neighborhood of \(q\) supports a smooth, single-valued minimizing branch of the inverse exponential \(\log_p\). Consequently, computations requiring such a branch cross their validity boundary.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A cut-locus encounter occurs when a point reaches the endpoint of maximal geodesic minimality from a base point, so a smooth single-valued minimizing logarithm is unavailable locally.
knowledge_statements.title: Cut-Locus Encounters

children.title: Distance-Smoothness Breakdown
children.top_down_role: Loss of smooth distance-based models near globally singular geometric regions.

knowledge_statements.title: Distance-Smoothness Breakdown
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Smoothness boundary for squared Riemannian distance from a fixed base point.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \((M,g)\) be a complete connected Riemannian manifold, fix \(p\in M\), and define \(h_p(q)=\tfrac12 d(p,q)^2\). On \(M\setminus\operatorname{Cut}(p)\), the minimizing logarithm is locally single-valued and \(h_p\) is smooth, with \(\operatorname{grad}h_p(q)=-\log_q(p)\). At a point \(q\in\operatorname{Cut}(p)\), this smooth representation fails: \(h_p\) is not smooth there, and the displayed classical gradient cannot be used as a smooth local field. Thus cut-locus contact is the validity boundary for distance-based smooth optimization models.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Squared distance from p is smooth away from p's cut locus, with gradient minus the logarithm toward p; at the cut locus this smooth model fails.
assumptions_latex: \((M,g)\) is complete and connected.
\(p\in M\) is fixed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The function \(h_p\) is smooth off \(\operatorname{Cut}(p)\) and loses smoothness on \(\operatorname{Cut}(p)\).

notation.meaning: Half the squared distance from p.
Minimizing logarithmic displacement from q to p.

review_flags: A source is required for the exact smoothness theorem for squared Riemannian distance and its gradient formula.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure-boundary kind fits the leaf, and the squared-distance gradient formula is internally consistent. No source with a theorem, section, or page locator supports smoothness off the cut locus and loss of smoothness on it, so the record cannot be accepted yet.

children.title: Geodesic-Selection Sensitivity
children.top_down_role: Dependence of computational behavior on the selected geodesic representative.

knowledge_statements.title: Geodesic-Selection Sensitivity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Antipodal points on a sphere show that quantities sampled along a minimizing geodesic can depend on its selection.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(p\in\mathbb S^2\), let \(q=-p\), and let \(u\in T_p\mathbb S^2\) satisfy \(\lVert u\rVert=1\). Every curve \(\gamma_u(t)=\cos(\pi t)p+\sin(\pi t)u\), \(0\leq t\leq1\), is a minimizing geodesic from \(p\) to \(q\). For a nonzero \(a\in T_p\mathbb S^2\) and \(f(z)=a^{\mathsf T}z\), one has \(f(\gamma_u(1/2))=a^{\mathsf T}u\). Thus an interpolation, model, or line-search quantity defined by choosing a minimizing geodesic between \(p\) and \(q\) is not intrinsic unless it is independent of \(u\) or a selection rule is specified.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At antipodal sphere points, different minimizing geodesics have different midpoints and objective values, so geodesic-based computations can depend on an unspecified selection.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathbb S^2\) carries its standard round metric.
\(a\in T_p\mathbb S^2\setminus\{0\}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f(\gamma_u(1/2))\) depends on the selected minimizing geodesic.

notation.meaning: minimizing geodesic selected by initial unit direction u

knowledge_statements.title: Incomplete-Manifold Escape
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A descent sequence can approach a missing finite-distance boundary point on an incomplete manifold.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider the Riemannian manifold \(M=(0,1)\) with the Euclidean metric and the smooth objective \(f(x)=x\). Starting from any \(x_0\in(0,1)\), define \(x_{k+1}=x_k/2\). Then \(f(x_{k+1})<f(x_k)\), \(f(x_k)\downarrow0=\inf_M f\), and the total path length satisfies \(\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}d(x_k,x_{k+1})=x_0<\infty\). Nevertheless, \((x_k)\) has no limit in \(M\), because its completion limit is the excluded point \(0\). Hence bounded objective values and finite travel do not ensure an accumulation point without completeness or an equivalent compactness condition.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: On the incomplete interval, a finite-length descent sequence approaches the missing endpoint and therefore has no limit within the manifold.
assumptions_latex: \(M=(0,1)\) has the metric induced from \(\mathbb R\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((x_k)\) is a finite-length descent sequence with no accumulation point in \(M\).

notation.meaning: Riemannian distance on the open interval

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The finite-length descent sequence is correct and appropriately classified as a counterexample, but the record has no source with a specific locator.

assumptions_latex: \(M=\mathbb R\) has its standard metric.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f(x_k)\downarrow \inf_M f\) while \((x_k)\) has no convergent subsequence.

notation.meaning: lower level set determined by the initial point

knowledge_statements.scope_note: A noncompact initial level set permits decreasing iterates to diverge while objective values approach the infimum.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(M=\mathbb R\) with its Euclidean metric and let \(f(x)=e^{-x}\). For \(x_0=0\), the lower level set \(L_0=\{x\in M:f(x)\leq f(x_0)\}=[0,\infty)\) is closed but noncompact. The sequence \(x_k=k\) remains in \(L_0\), satisfies \(f(x_{k+1})<f(x_k)\), and obeys \(f(x_k)\to 0=\inf_M f\). However, \(d(x_k,0)=k\to\infty\), so it has no convergent subsequence. Thus monotone descent and lower boundedness alone do not prevent escape when the relevant level set is noncompact.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A decreasing objective sequence can diverge to infinity inside a noncompact level set while its values converge to the infimum.
knowledge_statements.title: Noncompact Level-Set Escape

assumptions_latex: \(u\) and \(v\) lie in a common normal neighborhood of \(x\).
The curvature tensor and expansion remainder are bounded on that neighborhood.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Uniform tangent-model fidelity can fail when \(\lVert R_x\rVert r^2\) is not uniformly small.

notation.meaning: radius of the tangent-space model region

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Tangent-space Euclidean geometry need not approximate manifold geometry uniformly when curvature times squared model radius is not small.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(x\) lie in a Riemannian manifold and let \(u,v\in T_xM\) be sufficiently small normal-coordinate vectors. With a fixed curvature-sign convention, the squared-distance expansion has the form \[d(\operatorname{Exp}_x u,\operatorname{Exp}_x v)^2=\lVert u-v\rVert_x^2-\frac13\langle R_x(u,v)v,u\rangle_x+O((\lVert u\rVert_x+\lVert v\rVert_x)^5).\] Consequently, if \(\lVert R_x\rVert r^2\) is not uniformly small on a model region of radius \(r\), Euclidean distances and quadratic constructions in \(T_xM\) need not uniformly represent their manifold counterparts. Curvature control together with a radius below the normal-neighborhood scale is a standard sufficient condition for uniform local-model fidelity.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Tangent Euclidean models acquire curvature-dependent distance error; uniform fidelity can fail when curvature times the squared model radius is not small.
knowledge_statements.title: Curvature-Induced Model Distortion

assumptions_latex: \(L\) and \(R\) have full column rank \(r\).
\(F(L,R)=f(LR^{\mathsf T})\) is twice differentiable and gauge invariant.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Gauge directions lie in the representation differential's kernel and generate Hessian degeneracy at stationary representatives.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Redundant factor coordinates create null directions corresponding to gauge transformations that leave the represented point unchanged.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Represent a rank-\(r\) matrix by \(X=LR^{\mathsf T}\), with full-column-rank factors, under the gauge action \((L,R)\mapsto(LQ,RQ^{-\mathsf T})\) for \(Q\in\mathrm{GL}(r)\). For every \(\Omega\in\mathbb R^{r\times r}\), the vertical perturbation \((\delta L,\delta R)=(L\Omega,-R\Omega^{\mathsf T})\) satisfies \[\delta X=\delta L R^{\mathsf T}+L\delta R^{\mathsf T}=0.\] Hence any lifted invariant objective \(F(L,R)=f(LR^{\mathsf T})\) has zero directional derivative along every such perturbation, and at a stationary representative its coordinate Hessian has gauge-generated null directions. An unconstrained factor-space Newton system is therefore singular unless gauge directions are removed, fixed, or regularized.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Matrix factors contain gauge directions that change the factors but not their product, making invariant lifted Hessians singular at stationary points.
knowledge_statements.title: Gauge Degeneracy

assumptions_latex: \(X=LR^{\mathsf T}\neq0\).
The factor norms are induced by fixed Euclidean inner products.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Gauge-equivalent representations of the same \(X\) can have unbounded factor imbalance.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Gauge-equivalent factors can become arbitrarily unbalanced even though the represented matrix remains fixed.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X=LR^{\mathsf T}\neq0\) and, for \(\alpha>0\), define \(L_\alpha=\alpha L\) and \(R_\alpha=\alpha^{-1}R\). Then \(L_\alpha R_\alpha^{\mathsf T}=X\) for every \(\alpha\), whereas \(\lVert L_\alpha\rVert=\alpha\lVert L\rVert\) and \(\lVert R_\alpha\rVert=\alpha^{-1}\lVert R\rVert\). Thus the imbalance ratio \(\lVert L_\alpha\rVert/\lVert R_\alpha\rVert=\alpha^2\lVert L\rVert/\lVert R\rVert\) is unbounded as \(\alpha\to\infty\), although the represented matrix is unchanged. Consequently, Euclidean factor coordinates need not have uniformly controlled scaling across a gauge orbit.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Scaling one factor up and the other down leaves their product fixed but makes factor coordinates arbitrarily unbalanced.
knowledge_statements.title: Ill-Conditioned Factorizations

assumptions_latex: \(G\) acts freely and properly on \(\overline M\).
\(A\) is a smooth representative-space vector rule.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Failure of \(D\pi_{zg}A(zg)=D\pi_zA(z)\) makes the computation nonintrinsic.

notation.meaning: right action by the group element g

knowledge_statements.scope_note: A computation on representatives defines a quotient operation only when it is compatible with the group action.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let a Lie group \(G\) act freely and properly on a manifold \(\overline M\) from the right, with quotient map \(\pi:\overline M\to M=\overline M/G\). A representative-space vector rule \(A:\overline M\to T\overline M\) defines an unambiguous quotient vector field only if \[D\pi_{zg}A(zg)=D\pi_zA(z)\qquad\text{for every }z\in\overline M,\ g\in G.\] The stronger equivariance condition \(A(zg)=D(R_g)_zA(z)\) guarantees this equality. If two equivalent representatives violate the projected equality, then applying the rule and projecting produces different tangent vectors at the same quotient point; the computation is representation dependent and is not intrinsically defined on \(M\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A representative-level rule is invalid on a quotient when equivalent representatives produce different projected tangent vectors.
knowledge_statements.title: Noninvariant Computations

assumptions_latex: \(\overline M\to M\) has a specified horizontal–vertical splitting.
Stored quotient directions are represented by horizontal lifts.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Nonzero \(e_{k+1}^{\mathcal V}\) marks loss of the horizontal-lift invariant.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Approximate transport can introduce vertical components, invalidating formulas that assume stored directions remain horizontal lifts.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(T_z\overline M=\mathcal H_z\oplus\mathcal V_z\) be a horizontal–vertical splitting for a quotient manifold, and let \(P_z^{\mathcal H}\) denote horizontal projection. Suppose \(\xi_k\in\mathcal H_{z_k}\), but an approximate transport \(\widetilde{\mathcal T}_k:T_{z_k}\overline M\to T_{z_{k+1}}\overline M\) yields \[e_{k+1}^{\mathcal V}=(I-P_{z_{k+1}}^{\mathcal H})\widetilde{\mathcal T}_k\xi_k\neq0.\] Then \(\widetilde{\mathcal T}_k\xi_k\) is not the horizontal lift of its quotient projection. Without reprojecting or controlling \(\lVert e_{k+1}^{\mathcal V}\rVert\), formulas whose hypotheses require horizontal lifts do not apply directly to the stored direction.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A transport that does not preserve the horizontal distribution introduces vertical error and invalidates formulas whose hypotheses require horizontal lifts.
knowledge_statements.title: Horizontal-Lift Drift

assumptions_latex: \(f\) and \(R_x\) are twice differentiable.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The Hessian-only model mismatches \(f\circ R_x\) whenever \(\langle\operatorname{grad}f(x),a_x(\eta)\rangle_x\neq0\).

notation.meaning: covariant acceleration of the retraction curve at zero

knowledge_statements.scope_note: A Riemannian Hessian model matches the pullback model only when the retraction acceleration contribution vanishes or is included.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(R_x:T_xM\to M\) be a twice-differentiable retraction and set \(\widehat f_x=f\circ R_x\). For \(\eta\in T_xM\), let \(a_x(\eta)=\nabla_t\dot c(0)\), where \(c(t)=R_x(t\eta)\). Then \[D^2\widehat f_x(0)[\eta,\eta]=\langle\eta,\operatorname{Hess}f(x)[\eta]\rangle_x+\langle\operatorname{grad}f(x),a_x(\eta)\rangle_x.\] Therefore the tangent quadratic model using only the Riemannian Hessian is not the exact second-order Taylor model of the retraction pullback when the acceleration term is nonzero. Agreement holds at stationary points or for second-order retractions, but otherwise predicted and actual reductions may differ at quadratic order.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A first-order retraction contributes an acceleration term to the pullback Hessian, so a Hessian-only quadratic model may be mismatched.
knowledge_statements.title: Retraction–Model Mismatch

assumptions_latex: \(M\) is Riemannian.
\(\mathcal T_\eta\) is a vector transport associated with the retraction step \(R_x(\eta)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Uncontrolled \(\Delta_\eta\) destroys guaranteed preservation of metric-dependent quantities.

notation.meaning: vector transport along a retraction step

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Transported inner products and norms are reliable only under isometry or quantitatively controlled metric distortion.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(R_x(\eta)=y\) and let \(\mathcal T_\eta:T_xM\to T_yM\) be a vector transport. Define its metric defect by \[\Delta_\eta(u,v)=\langle\mathcal T_\eta u,\mathcal T_\eta v\rangle_y-\langle u,v\rangle_x.\] If \(\Delta_\eta\equiv0\), the transport is isometric and preserves norms, angles, and inner-product identities. If instead there exist admissible \(\eta,u\) with \(\lvert\Delta_\eta(u,u)\rvert\) uncontrolled relative to \(\lVert u\rVert_x^2\), then metric-dependent identities applied after transport have no guaranteed preservation. Such methods require isometric transport, explicit scaling, or uniform two-sided distortion bounds.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonisometric vector transport can distort norms and inner products, invalidating metric-dependent algorithmic identities unless the distortion is controlled.
knowledge_statements.title: Transport–Metric Incompatibility

assumptions_latex: \(g_k\in T_{x_k}M\) and \(H_k:T_{x_k}M\to T_{x_k}M\) is self-adjoint.
\(\eta_k\) and \(\eta_k^C\) satisfy the trust-region constraint.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Loss of a uniform Cauchy-decrease fraction removes the stated sufficient-decrease safeguard.

notation.meaning: Cauchy step for the tangent model

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Standard trust-region sufficient-decrease hypotheses are lost when approximate tangent steps do not achieve a uniform fraction of Cauchy decrease.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: At \(x_k\), consider the tangent trust-region model \(m_k(\eta)=f(x_k)+\langle g_k,\eta\rangle+\frac12\langle\eta,H_k\eta\rangle\) for \(\lVert\eta\rVert\leq\Delta_k\). Let \(\eta_k^{C}\) be a Cauchy step. A standard sufficient-accuracy condition is \[m_k(0)-m_k(\eta_k)\geq c\bigl(m_k(0)-m_k(\eta_k^{C})\bigr),\qquad c\in(0,1].\] If no uniform \(c>0\) exists, then this sufficient-decrease hypothesis is unavailable: the tangent solver may return feasible steps whose predicted decrease is an arbitrarily small fraction of the Cauchy decrease. A convergence conclusion then requires some alternative accuracy condition.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A feasible tangent step does not satisfy the standard sufficient-decrease safeguard when its predicted decrease is not a uniform fraction of Cauchy decrease.
knowledge_statements.title: Inaccurate Tangent-Subproblem Solutions

children.title: Derivative Conversion Inconsistency
children.top_down_role: Disagreement introduced during ambient, tangent, or Riemannian derivative conversion.

assumptions_latex: \(M\) is smoothly embedded in a finite-dimensional Euclidean ambient space \(E\).
\(G_x:E\to E\) is positive definite and defines the stated Riemannian metric on \(T_xM\).
\(\bar f\) is a smooth ambient extension of \(f\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A valid derivative conversion must satisfy \(\langle v_x,\eta\rangle_x=Df(x)[\eta]\) for all \(\eta\in T_xM\).

notation.meaning: ambient extension of the manifold objective

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Ambient derivatives must be converted using the same metric and tangent projection that define the manifold gradient.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(M\) be smoothly embedded in a finite-dimensional Euclidean space \(E\), let the metric satisfy \(\langle u,v\rangle_x=u^{\mathsf T}G_xv\) for \(u,v\in T_xM\), where \(G_x:E\to E\) is positive definite, and let \(P_x^{G}:E\to T_xM\) be the \(G_x\)-orthogonal projection. For a smooth ambient extension \(\bar f:E\to\mathbb R\), the Riemannian gradient is \[\operatorname{grad}f(x)=P_x^{G}G_x^{-1}\nabla\bar f(x),\] characterized by \(\langle\operatorname{grad}f(x),\eta\rangle_x=Df(x)[\eta]\) for every \(\eta\in T_xM\). Any conversion \(v_x\in T_xM\) that violates this identity is not the gradient of \(f\) under the declared geometry and need not be a descent direction.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Using a projection or inverse metric inconsistent with the declared geometry produces a vector that need not represent the objective derivative.
knowledge_statements.title: Derivative Conversion Inconsistency

children.title: Tangent Projection Inconsistency
children.top_down_role: Disagreement caused by inaccurate or incompatible tangent-space projections.

knowledge_statements.title: Tangent Projection Inconsistency
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Diagnostic condition for an ambient derivative projected onto an embedded manifold’s tangent space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(\mathcal M\subset\mathbb R^n\) be an embedded Riemannian manifold, let \(f:\mathcal M\to\mathbb R\) have a smooth extension \(\bar f\), and let \(P_x\) denote the orthogonal projection onto \(T_x\mathcal M\). For an implemented projection \(\widehat P_x\), tangent projection inconsistency at \(x\in\mathcal M\) means
\[
\widehat P_x\nabla \bar f(x)\ne P_x\nabla \bar f(x)=\operatorname{grad}f(x).
\]
A quantitative diagnostic is the defect \(\delta_x=\|\widehat P_x\nabla\bar f(x)-\operatorname{grad}f(x)\|_x\); inconsistency occurs exactly when \(\delta_x>0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The implemented tangent projection is inconsistent when projecting the ambient gradient does not produce the intrinsic Riemannian gradient at the same point.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal M\subset\mathbb R^n\) is a smooth embedded manifold with the induced metric.
\(f\) admits a differentiable ambient extension near \(x\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\widehat P_x\nabla\bar f(x)\ne\operatorname{grad}f(x)\iff\delta_x>0\).

notation.meaning: Orthogonal projection onto the tangent space at x.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The condition is mathematically coherent and fits the failure-taxonomy leaf, but no citation supports the named diagnostic or its manifold-specific formulation.

children.title: Derivative–Projection Compatibility Failures
children.top_down_role: Failures arising when derivative conversion is incompatible with the projection convention.

knowledge_statements.title: Derivative–Projection Compatibility Failures
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Compatibility boundary between an ambient derivative representation and an implemented tangent projection.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(\mathcal M\subset\mathbb R^n\) be an embedded Riemannian manifold with the induced metric, let \(f:\mathcal M	o\mathbb R\) have a differentiable extension \( ar f\), and let \(P_x:\mathbb R^n	o T_x\mathcal M\) be the orthogonal projection. For an ambient derivative approximation \(D_x\in\mathbb R^n\) and an implemented projection \(\widehat P_x:\mathbb R^n	o T_x\mathcal M\), define the compatibility defect by \[E_x:=\widehat P_xD_x-\operatorname{grad}f(x).\] The pair is compatible at \(x\) exactly when \(E_x=0\), and compatibility fails when \(E_x
e0\). If \(D_x=
abla ar f(x)+e_x\) and \(\widehat P_x=P_x+\Delta_x\), then \[E_x=P_xe_x+\Delta_x
abla ar f(x)+\Delta_xe_x.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Derivative–projection compatibility fails when the implemented projection of the ambient derivative approximation differs from the intrinsic Riemannian gradient.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal M\subset\mathbb R^n\) is an embedded Riemannian manifold with the induced metric.
\(f\) has a differentiable ambient extension \(\bar f\).
\(\widehat P_xD_x\in T_x\mathcal M\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(E_x\ne0\) is the derivative–projection compatibility failure condition.

notation.meaning: Ambient derivative approximation used by the method.

children.title: Representation-Dependent Diagnostic Drift
children.top_down_role: Diagnostic variation across equivalent manifold representations or gauge choices.

knowledge_statements.title: Representation-Dependent Diagnostic Drift
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure of an ostensibly intrinsic diagnostic to remain invariant under equivalent representations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(\phi:U\to V\) be a change of coordinates or equivalent manifold representation, with \(y=\phi(x)\). Suppose diagnostics \(d_U(x)\) and \(d_V(y)\) are intended to measure the same intrinsic residual. Representation-dependent diagnostic drift occurs when
\[
d_U(x)\ne d_V(\phi(x)).
\]
For vector residuals \(r_U(x)\in T_x\mathcal M\) and \(r_V(y)\in T_y\mathcal M\), the coordinate-compatible condition is \(r_V(\phi(x))=D\phi(x)r_U(x)\); its failure defines vector diagnostic drift.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Diagnostic drift occurs when equivalent coordinates or representations yield unequal scalar diagnostics, or vector residuals that do not transform by the representation map’s differential.
assumptions_latex: \(\phi\) is a diffeomorphism between two representations of the same manifold region.
The compared diagnostics are intended to encode one intrinsic quantity.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(d_U(x)\ne d_V(\phi(x))\) or \(r_V(\phi(x))\ne D\phi(x)r_U(x)\) signals representation-dependent drift.

notation.meaning: Change of coordinates or equivalent representation.
Scalar diagnostics in the two representations.
Vector residuals in the two representations.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The scalar invariance and vector equivariance tests are coherent and fit the leaf, but the named diagnostic and its intended class of equivalent representations lack supporting evidence.

children.title: Saddle-Point Attraction
children.top_down_role: Iterative behavior that remains near saddle-type critical regions.

knowledge_statements.title: Saddle-Point Attraction
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Convergence of an optimization trajectory to a nonminimizing stationary point.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(F:\mathcal M\to\mathcal M\) be the iteration map \(x_{k+1}=F(x_k)\) for minimizing \(f\). Saddle-point attraction occurs from \(x_0\) when there exists \(x_\star\in\mathcal M\) such that \(x_k\to x_\star\), \(\operatorname{grad}f(x_\star)=0\), and the Riemannian Hessian has a negative-curvature direction:
\[
\exists v\in T_{x_\star}\mathcal M\setminus\{0\}:\quad \langle v,\operatorname{Hess}f(x_\star)[v]\rangle_{x_\star}<0.
\]
The attraction set is \(\mathcal A(x_\star)=\{x_0:F^k(x_0)\to x_\star\}\); the failure is realized whenever \(x_0\in\mathcal A(x_\star)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A method exhibits saddle-point attraction when its iterates converge to a stationary point possessing a strictly negative Riemannian-curvature direction.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) is twice continuously differentiable on the Riemannian manifold \(\mathcal M\).
The iterates remain defined and converge.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x_0\in\mathcal A(x_\star)\) with negative Hessian curvature implies convergence to a nonminimum stationary point.

notation.meaning: Attraction set of the stationary point.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The record precisely defines attraction to a strict saddle and fits the failure leaf, but no source supports this selected strict-saddle version in the manifold setting.

children.title: Flat-Plateau Stagnation
children.top_down_role: Slow progress across weakly varying or nearly degenerate landscape regions.

knowledge_statements.title: Flat-Plateau Stagnation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-time stagnation diagnostic on a region with uniformly small gradient and curvature.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(x_0,\ldots,x_K\in\mathcal M\) be iterates for minimizing a twice differentiable function \(f\). Given tolerances \(\varepsilon_g,\varepsilon_H,\varepsilon_s>0\), flat-plateau stagnation over this segment means
\[
\max_{0\le k\le K}\|\operatorname{grad}f(x_k)\|_{x_k}\le\varepsilon_g,\qquad
\max_{0\le k<K}d(x_{k+1},x_k)\le\varepsilon_s,
\]
and \(\|\operatorname{Hess}f(x_k)\|_{\mathrm{op}}\le\varepsilon_H\) for every \(k\), while the segment has not reached the prescribed objective or solution-accuracy target.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Flat-plateau stagnation is a finite iterate segment with small gradients, curvature, and steps, yet without attaining the required solution accuracy.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) is twice differentiable along the iterate segment.
A target accuracy and positive diagnostic tolerances are fixed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The displayed small-gradient, small-step, and small-curvature conditions without target attainment constitute plateau stagnation.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The finite-segment diagnostic is internally coherent, but its simultaneous gradient, Hessian, and step thresholds are a nonstandard taxonomy choice without cited support.

children.title: Saddle–Plateau Transition Regimes
children.top_down_role: Landscape regions where saddle behavior merges with extended flat geometry.

knowledge_statements.title: Saddle–Plateau Transition Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Local regime where weak negative curvature approaches the flat-curvature boundary at algorithmic resolution.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal M\) be a finite-dimensional Riemannian manifold, let \(x_k\in\mathcal M\), let \(g_k=\operatorname{grad}f(x_k)\), and let \(\lambda_k\) be the smallest eigenvalue of the self-adjoint operator \(\operatorname{Hess}f(x_k)\). For tolerances \(\varepsilon_g,\varepsilon_H>0\), a saddle–plateau transition regime is characterized by \[\|g_k\|_{x_k}\le\varepsilon_g,\qquad -\varepsilon_H\le\lambda_k\le0.\] Thus the point is approximately stationary and its weak negative or zero curvature lies within the chosen curvature-resolution threshold. A sequence approaches the transition boundary when \(\|g_k\|_{x_k}\to0\) and \(\lambda_k\uparrow0\) through negative values.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The transition regime contains nearly stationary points whose weakest curvature is nonpositive but lies within the resolution threshold, ranging from weak saddle curvature to the flat boundary.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal M\) is finite dimensional.
\(f\) is twice differentiable near the considered iterates.
\(\operatorname{Hess}f(x_k)\) is self-adjoint on \(T_{x_k}\mathcal M\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\|g_k\|_{x_k}\le\varepsilon_g\) and \(-\varepsilon_H\le\lambda_k\le0\) define the saddle–plateau transition regime.

notation.meaning: Riemannian gradient at the kth iterate.
Smallest eigenvalue of the Riemannian Hessian.

children.title: Escape-Mechanism Failure Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Regimes where perturbative, curvature-based, or stochastic escape mechanisms lose effectiveness.

knowledge_statements.title: Escape-Mechanism Failure Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary where permitted perturbation or negative-curvature steps cannot produce a required local decrease.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal M\) be a finite-dimensional Riemannian manifold, let \(x\in\mathcal M\) satisfy \(\|\operatorname{grad}f(x)\|_x\le\varepsilon_g\), and let an escape mechanism permit tangent steps \(s\in T_x\mathcal M\) with \(\|s\|_x\le\rho\), followed by a retraction \(R_x(s)\). Assume \(f\circ R_x\) is continuous on this closed ball. For a required decrease \(\Delta>0\), the mechanism succeeds locally when some admissible step satisfies \(f(R_x(s))\le f(x)-\Delta\). Its local failure condition is \[\min_{\|s\|_x\le\rho}f(R_x(s))>f(x)-\Delta.\] At this boundary, no permitted step achieves the required decrease.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An escape mechanism fails locally when every permitted tangent step followed by retraction gives objective value strictly above the required-decrease threshold.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal M\) is finite dimensional.
\(R\) is a retraction on \(\mathcal M\).
\(f\circ R_x\) is continuous on \(\{s\in T_x\mathcal M:\|s\|_x\le\rho\}\).
Positive thresholds \(\varepsilon_g,\rho,\Delta\) are fixed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\min_{\|s\|_x\le\rho}f(R_x(s))>f(x)-\Delta\) is the local escape-failure condition.

children.title: Stochastic Variance Explosion
children.top_down_role: Regimes where estimator variability overwhelms useful manifold search information.

knowledge_statements.title: Stochastic Variance Explosion
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Loss of uniform second-moment control for a stochastic Riemannian gradient estimator.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(G(x,\xi)\in T_x\mathcal M\) be a stochastic estimator of \(\operatorname{grad}f(x)\), and set \(b(x)=\mathbb E[G(x,\xi)]-\operatorname{grad}f(x)\). Its conditional variance is
\[
V(x)=\mathbb E\!\left[\|G(x,\xi)-\mathbb E[G(x,\xi)]\|_x^2\mid x\right].
\]
Variance explosion along iterates \((x_k)\) means \(\sup_k V(x_k)=\infty\), or, for a parameterized sampling regime, \(V(x_k)\to\infty\). This violates the uniform bounded-variance hypothesis commonly used to control accumulated stochastic error.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Variance explosion occurs when the centered second moment of stochastic tangent-gradient estimates becomes unbounded along the iterates or sampling regime.
assumptions_latex: \(G(x,\xi)\) is measurable and tangent-valued.
The displayed conditional second moments exist, possibly with value \(+\infty\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\sup_k V(x_k)=\infty\) defines stochastic variance explosion along the iterate sequence.

notation.meaning: Conditional centered second moment of the estimator.
Estimator bias relative to the Riemannian gradient.

children.title: Stochastic Bias Explosion
children.top_down_role: Regimes where systematic estimator error dominates the intended geometric direction.

knowledge_statements.title: Stochastic Bias Explosion
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Unbounded systematic error in a stochastic Riemannian gradient estimator.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(G(x,\xi)\in T_x\mathcal M\) estimate \(\operatorname{grad}f(x)\). Define its conditional bias by
\[
b(x)=\mathbb E[G(x,\xi)\mid x]-\operatorname{grad}f(x).
\]
Bias explosion along iterates \((x_k)\) means \(\sup_k\|b(x_k)\|_{x_k}=\infty\), or \(\|b(x_k)\|_{x_k}\to\infty\) in an asymptotic sampling regime. More generally, convergence-oriented bias control fails whenever the weighted bias is nonsummable, such as \(\sum_k\alpha_k\|b(x_k)\|_{x_k}=\infty\) for step sizes \(\alpha_k>0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Bias explosion is unbounded systematic gradient-estimation error; a weaker convergence failure occurs when step-size-weighted bias is not summable.
assumptions_latex: \(G(x,\xi)\) is integrable and tangent-valued.
The iterates and positive step sizes \(\alpha_k\) are defined.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\sup_k\|b(x_k)\|_{x_k}=\infty\) gives bias explosion, while \(\sum_k\alpha_k\|b(x_k)\|_{x_k}=\infty\) violates summable-bias control.

children.title: Variance–Bias Coupling
children.top_down_role: Interactions through which variance control alters bias or bias reduction amplifies variability.

knowledge_statements.title: Variance–Bias Coupling
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Mean-square error decomposition for a stochastic tangent-gradient estimator at a fixed point.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Fix \(x\in\mathcal M\) and let \(G(x,\xi)\in T_x\mathcal M\) be square-integrable. With \(g=\operatorname{grad}f(x)\), \(\mu=\mathbb E[G(x,\xi)\mid x]\), and \(b=\mu-g\), the conditional mean-square estimation error decomposes as
\[
\mathbb E[\|G(x,\xi)-g\|_x^2\mid x]
=
\mathbb E[\|G(x,\xi)-\mu\|_x^2\mid x]+\|b\|_x^2.
\]
Consequently, controlling only variance cannot control total estimator error when bias is large, and controlling only bias cannot control it when variance is large.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At a fixed manifold point, stochastic gradient mean-square error equals centered variance plus squared bias; either component can prevent estimator accuracy.
assumptions_latex: \(G(x,\xi)\) is square-integrable in the single tangent inner-product space \(T_x\mathcal M\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{MSE}_x(G)=\operatorname{Var}_x(G)+\|b\|_x^2\).

notation.meaning: Conditional bias relative to the Riemannian gradient.
Riemannian gradient at the fixed point.

children.title: Sampling-Regime Instability
children.top_down_role: Batch, subsampling, or data-distribution regimes producing unstable stochastic behavior.

knowledge_statements.title: Sampling-Regime Instability
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure of stochastic-estimator moment controls under changing sample size or sampling distribution.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(G_k=G(x_k,\xi_k;m_k,q_k)\in T_{x_k}\mathcal M\) be an estimator using batch size \(m_k\) and sampling law \(q_k\). Define conditional bias \(b_k=\mathbb E[G_k\mid x_k]-\operatorname{grad}f(x_k)\) and variance \(V_k=\mathbb E[\|G_k-\mathbb E[G_k\mid x_k]\|_{x_k}^2\mid x_k]\). Sampling-regime instability occurs when admissible changes in \((m_k,q_k)\) destroy required uniform controls, for example
\[
\sup_k V_k=\infty
\quad\text{or}\quad
\sum_k\alpha_k\|b_k\|_{x_k}=\infty.
\]
These failures invalidate convergence arguments requiring bounded variance and summable weighted bias.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Sampling is unstable when changing batch sizes or sampling laws destroys the variance or bias controls required by the stochastic method.
assumptions_latex: Each \(G_k\) is conditionally integrable and tangent-valued.
The method specifies positive step sizes \(\alpha_k\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Unbounded \(V_k\) or nonsummable \(\alpha_k\|b_k\|_{x_k}\) marks sampling-regime instability.

notation.meaning: Conditional variance and bias of the estimator.

knowledge_statements.title: Metric-Induced Ill-Conditioning
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Poor conditioning caused by the chosen Riemannian metric rather than solely by the objective.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(x_\star\) be a nondegenerate local minimizer of \(f:\mathcal M\to\mathbb R\) under a Riemannian metric \(g\), and let \(H_g=\operatorname{Hess}_g f(x_\star)\) be positive definite and self-adjoint on \(T_{x_\star}\mathcal M\). Its metric-dependent spectral condition number is \[\kappa_g(H_g)=\frac{\lambda_{\max}(H_g)}{\lambda_{\min}(H_g)}.\] For a family of admissible metrics \((g_\theta)\), metric-induced ill-conditioning occurs when \(\kappa_{g_\theta}(H_{g_\theta})\) is large or unbounded while another admissible metric yields a bounded condition number. The adverse conditioning is then attributable to the metric choice within the specified family.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Metric-induced ill-conditioning occurs when the chosen Riemannian metric makes the Hessian condition number large or unbounded although another admissible metric in the comparison family keeps it bounded.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) is twice differentiable near a nondegenerate local minimizer \(x_\star\).
Each considered metric makes the corresponding Hessian positive definite and self-adjoint.
The compared metrics belong to a specified admissible family.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Large or unbounded \(\kappa_{g_\theta}(H_{g_\theta})\) relative to another admissible metric identifies metric-induced ill-conditioning within the comparison family.

notation.meaning: Spectral condition number measured using metric g.
Member of an admissible metric family.

knowledge_statements.title: Premature Rank-Boundary Approach
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Fixed-rank matrix-manifold failure regime characterized before first-order stationarity is attained.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(\mathcal M_r=\{X\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}:\operatorname{rank}(X)=r\}\), where \(1\le r<\min\{m,n\}\), and let \(f:\mathcal M_r\to\mathbb R\) be continuously differentiable. A sequence \((X_k)\subset\mathcal M_r\) exhibits premature rank-boundary approach if
\[\sigma_r(X_k)\to0\quad\text{and}\quad\liminf_{k\to\infty}\|\operatorname{grad}f(X_k)\|_{X_k}>0.\]
Thus every accumulation point in the ambient matrix space has rank strictly below \(r\), while the iterates remain uniformly separated from first-order stationarity on \(\mathcal M_r\). Consequently, any convergence guarantee requiring the iterates to remain in a compact subset of \(\mathcal M_r\), or requiring uniformly well-conditioned local coordinates, retractions, or tangent-space representations, is inapplicable without an additional boundary-avoidance condition.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The iterates approach rank deficiency while their Riemannian gradient stays nonzero, invalidating convergence arguments that require stationarity, compact containment inside the fixed-rank manifold, or uniformly conditioned local geometry.
assumptions_latex: \(f:\mathcal M_r\to\mathbb R\) is continuously differentiable.
\((X_k)\subset\mathcal M_r\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\sigma_r(X_k)\to0\) together with \(\liminf_k\|\operatorname{grad}f(X_k)\|_{X_k}>0\) identifies a nonstationary approach to the lower-rank boundary and defeats convergence hypotheses requiring uniform separation from that boundary.

notation.meaning: Manifold of real matrices having rank exactly r.
Smallest nonzero singular value of a rank-r matrix X.
Riemannian gradient under the chosen smooth metric on the fixed-rank manifold.

Authoritative source needed for the selected failure-regime formulation and its conditioning consequences.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure_boundary kind fits this terminal failure-regime container, and the rank-boundary implication is mathematically plausible. However, no citation is supplied, and the inventory contains no relevant fixed-rank manifold source. An authoritative source with a specific locator is required for this named failure regime and especially for the broad claim that local coordinates, retractions, or tangent-space representations necessarily lose uniform conditioning. The Riemannian metric governing the gradient norm must also be specified sufficiently to support the nonstationarity condition near the boundary.
